hint.name: SCG Vegas - Avatar of Fire
hint.primer:
This is a midrange deck that uses defensive sites and 4+ power minions to slowly take control of the realm. It plays defensively early with Root Spiders and Pudge to lock down sites that the opponent can attack, and ramps to 5+ power minions to finish the game.


Site placement is very important for this deck. Pebbled Paths, Varmint Warrens, Gnome Hollows, River of Flame, etc, all significantly change how/where the opponent will position their minions. Forge and Bedrock provide some protection against Atlantean Fate and flooding, and it is often ok to create a lance underground for a Root Spider to equip. Varmint Warrens are especially good, as your beasts cannot be attacked or targeted there. Philosopher's Stone and Shrine of the Dragonlord enables 6 and 7 mana whilst not adding more vulnerable sites to the board.


This deck runs 37 minions, and 17 of them are beasts/dragons, which make Firebreathing a great removal tool, in addition to the standard Bury, Earthquake, and Infiltrate. Direct damage via Vile Imps, Dragonettes, Ring of Morrigan, and a single Wildfire let's us clear out a path for our attacks or wake up Slumbering Giantess. Boneyard also shines with lots of great targets to reanimate, while Pillar of Zeiros and Funeral Pyre can make the effect stronger in our favor. Royal Bodyguard is the MVP when it comes to surviving on DD.


Lastly, the deck runs 16 fire sites and 16 earth sites, so manage them carefully. AoF represents Fireball with any fire site in hand, and can clear blockers, activate Ignis Rex's ability, and finish the game off of DD. You only need 3 fire and 2 earth to cast all your spells.


There's more tricks that are in the deck, but I leave it to you to discover and take advantage of them. Enjoy!

Seeing Red - 1st place SCG Con Baltimore and NYC Cornerstone 2025
hint.primer:
Seeing Red

Primer by UnderSietch


*UPDATE*


I’ve updated this decklist to reflect the one I played in the SCG CON Baltimore 2025, where I took 1st place. I've also update the primer for the new list and added more specific examples of how I play special cards, artifacts and auras in addition to the turn by turn card flow breakdown. Thank you for your interest and your feedback!


*NEW* Video of the Quarter Finals Match from SCG Con in Baltimore 2025 vs Count Tolstoy


Feature article on Sorcery TCG about Seeing Red and it's pilot, yours truly!


Video of the Championship Match at SCG CON in Baltimore 2025


Interview on Common Sense Sorcery Podcast about my win at SCG CON Baltimore


Team Covenant play-tests this deck on their YouTube channel ahead of SCG CON Houston! (gameplay at 50 mins)


Check out the video of the final match of the NYC King of the Realm cornerstone!


Introduction:


I'm typically a very whimsical deck builder. I like the story and the artwork and the intricate interactions between the weirdest and coolest cards. I often even write a little bit of lore to explain the narrative of the "characters" in my deck and how they came together to do battle against strange and ominous enemies. What can I say? I'm a nerd.


But with the tournament season approaching, I've been noticing an uptick in a more competitive and aggressive play-style all around me. This deck is a response to getting my butt relentlessly kicked over and over by some very good players and deck builders in my local community, who were tuning their tournament decks at our casual meetups. The calculated and efficient competition deck is a new adventure and mindset for me. And I think a good amount of beginners luck, mixed with being thrown to the wolves (sometimes literally) again and again, led to my winning our NYC cornerstone recently. I had been so tilted, so often, that I was literally SEEING RED.


Philosophy:


I decided that I wanted to make my games as short and sweet as possible. I don't want to allow other decks to get set up and start to hit me with big, intricate plays. My goal is to get my opponent in a reactive space, having to spend their precious few actions each game removing my threats and adapting to my board position, rather than imposing their will.


Playstyle:


I chose Mono-Fire because it's a fast and nasty suit. There are plenty of places to find extra damage for removal and to lower my opponents life total, while leaving me in an advantageous board-state. And it's very low cost!


I chose the Druid as my avatar for one reason: An immortal, airborne spellcaster, TAWNY. Flying around and dealing Fire's unblockable Area of Effect (AoE) damage to both remove enemy threats and deal damage to enemy avatars simultaneously.


The basic idea behind the deck is to combine the sometimes self-destructing damage from tawny, and genesis damage from deserts, with genesis and end-of-turn bonus damage from fire minion cards to remove enemy threats and deal damage without spending mana or losing my minions in a fight.


For example:


Opponent plays an Autumn Unicorn on turn 3.

I attack it with Tawny (she dies, but there's one damage), I play a desert (one damage and summon Tawny again, she's back!), and I play a vile imp for 2 mana and the genesis damage removes the Unicorn and leaves my Imp and Tawny alive. The board now has two threats on it for me and none for them.


Tawny's bonus damage also works in the reverse. You can cast an AoE spell, then attack with Tawny to deal one damage to an enemy minion THEN cast a desert to deal one additional damage and summon Tawny again for no cost.


For example:


Opponent drops a Atlas Wanderers on turn 4 due to a Mana boost from a Gothic Tower.

I cast Firebolts with Tawny, then attack the Atlas Wanderers with Tawny dealing a 4th damage, then I tap my Druid to play a Desert nearby, dealing the Atlas Wanderers a 5th and fatal damage and summoning Tawny again for no cost.


This allows me to destroy my opponents 5-cost drop with a total expenditure of 2 mana.


The last and most important note I'll make about our magical owl friend is that she's actually the perfect foil to your Druid opponents. By using a Torshammar Trinket, you can still have Tawny fly around near your opponent's avatar when they are Flipped and Bruin is active. Now that she's a 2 power, she can take steps nearby your opponents Druid and not die from their special ability. Then, she can cast a kill spell.


Use your owl. Give it a Torshammar Trinket and hit your opponents sites as often as possible. Cast Boudicca and give Tawny a Trinket and hit your opponent's sites with your owl for 5 damage. Be very active and rude with your bird friend. If your opponent is spending cards and mana removing your owl, you are winning. They are spending time, energy and resource on something that you get for free. Try your best to get them to react to your owl.


For me? The Bruin is a "smash in case of emergency" card. I want to spend most games not needing it. I want to be able to cast tawny by playing a site all game long. She's that important.



How and when to play:


You need to be patient!

(read that again)


This deck allows you to win FAST. I've observed that, in many games, Sorcery players cast anywhere from 12-18 spells and it can take up to 50 minutes to finish. In my games, my opponents cast 7-10 spells and the game can be over in 25 minutes.


(Which resulted in a very nice long break between rounds for me at the tournaments)


That doesn't mean that you play all of your cards out fast, however. Quite the contrary. It means you need to make every point of damage count. Hit their sites and Avatars early and as often as possible, yes. BUT DO NOT EMPTY YOUR HAND. You are leading the action while tactically responding to their drops. Find ways to remove their drop and increase your board presence AND deal them a little damage each turn. It's very possible. But you are most likely playing only one spell per turn. Your owl, deserts, genesis effects and end of turn effects will make it feel like you're doing much more than that but you're not. It's very simple and very deadly. And you'll need spells in your hand if your opponent manages to slow the game down and draw things out.



Turn by turn:


Mulligan:


You want a removal or control spell like Disintegrate, Immolation or Infiltrate in your hand ideally, and at least one cheap minion and one fire damage spell. Having three minions isn't the end of the world. You can have a War Horse, Colicky Dragonettes and Saracen Raiders and play forward from a really good place. The removal and fire magics will show up when you need them.


Make sure you have a Forge and at least one Desert in your hand, trust me. If you can't do that, make sure you have two fire threshold in your opening hand. Sinkholes and Wizard's Dens are awesome, don't mulligan them unless you have multiples in hand.


Ideal sample hand:


Disintegrate, War Horse, Minor Explosion

Forge, Red Desert, Poison Well



Turn by turn breakdown:


Turn 1: play the forge, make the lance, create Tawny and have her pick up the lance.


Turn 2: If you went first, Play a Bonfire or a Funeral Pyre or something forward toward your opponent and drop the War Horse and step Tawny forward to hand the lance off to your other minion. You don't always get the charge or genesis effects of minions and sites to land, that doesn't mean it's a bad play. Remember you're increasing your board presence with each drop and they'll have to spend resources to clear those spells, which you'll replace with more powerful ones as you draw them. Of course the best sites to play forward in a central position would be a Sinkhole, Smokestacks or Vesuvius. But we can't always get what we want.


If you went second, try dropping that Poisoned Well and get a hit on their life total, if they played forward toward you. Or play a Sinkhole forward to prepare for any unwanted sites. Wizard's Den is also a fantastic starting site, or a drop on turn three on your back row to get the extra spell draw.


Going second also means you can bring the lance up from Tawny, hand it off to the War Horse and immediately step forward to deal 3 first-strike damage to either a minion or, ideally, your opponent's site.


NOTE: You will draw spells and play the sites from your hand on the first three turns.


Turn 3: I love the Redcap Powries here, or even a Trinket on Tawny and Firebolts for removal or direct damage to the enemy avatar (that's 5 damage turn 3). When in doubt, Minor Explosion is the best, most effective card in this deck. I honestly have considered adding a 4th copy recently. Explode everything all of the time. Do not hesitate to do damage. It's your whole job. Do it often. Colicky Dragonettes are good here. Save your Kobolds for later unless there's an obvious play that maximizes their end of turn strike ability.



Turn 4: You will draw and play a site. This leaves you with four sites on the board and three or four spells in hand. Great cards open up on this turn: Saracen Raiders is an awesome free 3 damage on an unprotected and unsuspecting opponent's site. Infiltrate becomes an option, but I typically save this until my opponent drops something that seems like a game-changing bomb. Think Pudge Butcher or Seirawan Hydra. These are the things you want to take and tap down and keep them out of the game. Redcap Powries with a Torshammer Trinket is a favorite of mine to remove a 4 power minion or strike a site for 4. Boudicca opens up on Turn 4, but don't drop her on the board unless Tawny and/or another minion can undoubtedly strike a site freely. Her ability is too good to waste. If you play Boudicca back and away from the fray, you may get multiple turns with her ability in play and swing the game heavily in your favor.



Turn 5: draw a spell and tap to draw a site. The only reason you would draw a site to play here is if you already have Rebecks in your hand and you see a good opportunity to use your charge giant to get a big hit in on your opponent. Otherwise, stick to the plan so you can have 5 sites next turn.


Turn 6: Draw a spell and play your 5th site. This should leave you with 3 or 4 spells in hand and five sites on the board. You can play everything in the deck besides Infernal Legion with this board state. This is where the world opens up to you. Try to spread your minions out as much as possible so that they're more difficult to remove. Your opponent is going to scratch and claw to stabilize. There may be temptation at times to play multiple cards from your own hand. Only do this if it lands your opponent at death's door or decisively swings the game toward your win.


Turn 7: Draw a spell and tap to draw a site. Now you have all of the sites that you'll ever need and you have three or 4 spells in hand. This is what I mean by BE PATIENT. You'll find yourself in a remarkable board state with plenty of spells in hand. If you can leverage your extra damage well, you might still have two or three threats on the board at this point.



How to Deal Damage:


Every time that you can, play a minion with charge and hit your opponent's sites. Every time that you can, cast fire spells that hit their avatar or groups of minions. By turn 5 or 6, you may have taken half of their life total away by chipping away with Tawny, fire damage and minions hitting sites.


I usually find that I'm holding more immediate damage threats than my opponent. If I consistently am hitting them once per turn for 3+ damage, I get them a little off their game and they start to have to waste resources and dig for answers.


Try not to win more. Win just enough. You really want those three spells in hand to deal with some of the game's inherent big swings.


How to win:


You didn't flip your Druid, did you? Good. Being able to summon Tawny (and maybe put a Trinket on her) and get her into position to deal a Minor Explosion, Firebreathing, Lava Flow, Firebolts or Firebreathing is your ticket to victory. Good players keep a kill in their hand when they can. If you can hold onto one of these spells and not use it until you get your opponent to death's door, you'll have a tidy and efficient victory on your hands.


Remove their threats when they're on death's door. Get rid of their minions, and clear your path. Sometimes you don't have the fire spell and you need superior numbers of minions to get a strike in. Don't forget to remove their blockers to make a charge minion very deadly.


Sometimes, walking your druid forward and then flipping for Bruin and your special ability, can pin their Avatar down when it's on deaths door and keep it from being able to run away from your fire damage. In this case only, you don't need Tawny, because your Avatar is your spellcaster.



Special cards and their uses:


Your damage (most of it) comes from your small minions and fire spells from Tawny. But sometimes you need to be able to flex into a more midrange role and become a bigger beast to seal the deal against a powerful opponent.


There are a few HUGE drops in this deck that help you out a lot.


Rebecks is my favorite card here, dealing 4 damage to an opponent's site on the same turn that you play it. Pair him with a Torshammer Trinket or Jihad for a bigger swing. Have him ride a warhorse to get him into a deeper and more problematic position for an opponent. On a later turn, use a fire spell to clear out a blocker before dropping Rebecks to get a free hit on your opponent's site.


Boudicca on turn 4 when you have Tawny and maybe a War Horse and a Redcap Powries on the board? Do some math here, that's 15 damage if they all go unblocked to your opponent's sites. Normally I play her very carefully away from the battle. But sometimes she can create a very welcome distraction. While your opponent focuses on removing her, you can keep hitting for 2-5 damage per turn on their life total. Remember the goal is to get them to door and ping them for the win. If you lose cards and life along the way, so be it. Don't win more! Just win. Never waste resources to save a special card.


Siege Giants are amazing. These guys are why I don't have to play Blaze or Mad Dash in this deck. I get all of the movement I need from these dudes. They can throw 21 of the cards in this deck (including Avatar and Tawny), to any nearby site without having to tap for the ability. They can even throw a War Horse that they themselves are riding. READ THAT AGAIN. They can saddle up on a horse, throw that horse diagonally, then both the horse and the giant still can take a step and declare an attack. Use Siege Giant to spread your damage out far and wide, like a joyful flaming trebuchet.


Monstrous Lion's job is actually as a removal spell. I use it to deal a surprise and tidy four damage to an enemy that's on my border or in my territory. Sometimes a BattleMage or some other antsy Avatar gets too close and catches a lion to the face. Don't expect the Lion to live for more than one turn very often. Add a Torshammer Trinket on turn 5 or later for extra Lion.


Askelon Phoenix is in the deck to provide air support and fire resistance. You'll very rarely use its ability to power it up. But it takes no damage from fire spells, minions or abilities. It survives a poison nova. Heck, it survives a direct strike from Ignis Rex holding Crown of the Victor. It's a good card, and is usually a sort of turret or defensive/support play for me, more so than a beatdown.


Infernal Legion has never been invited to a party. Nobody likes to see this thing hit the board. It's an absolutely enormous problem for most opponents. But be careful, it's also trouble for you if you don't play it right. This is another card I'd qualify as a late game or defensive bailout play.



Artifacts and Auras:


The Ring of Morrigan is the most efficient card in the game. I think it has to go in any deck right now. Its overall effect is that of a desert that can be triggered every turn and gains you life for each damage you do with it. Enjoy your bling.


Torshammer Trinket is very powerful. There is absolutely an argument for playing a third one of these in the deck and playing at 52 cards. Your opponent cannot interact with it unless they make you discard it from your hand. It can be placed on any minion or avatar in order to increase its power by 1 on your turn. Another little added single damage to reinforce the soul of the deck. Happy smashing.


Mask of Mayhem is a very tricky play. Be careful. I'd recommend dropping it when you have 2-3 minions nearby each other. Maybe one of them removes a large minion and the other two get a free hit that's big. If you can wipe the board and maybe follow it up with some Saracen Raiders or another charge minion? Go ahead. But be hyper aware that this also benefits your opponent. Battlemages love this being on the board and so do Avatars of Earth.


Drums of Doom is the one big defensive card I have in the deck. If all goes to heck and you need to protect yourself from minions, put Drums on your Avatar and flip for Bruin. Your thorns ability will now deal lethal damage to any potential nefarious trespassers.


Jihad - If you can cast Jihad on your opponent's side of the board, this deck gets very hard to deal with. This aura opens up all of your extra damage genesis and end of turn affects from minions, hitting the enemy's avatar the very first turn they're played. Don't hesitate to do damage to their life total. Take them to death's door as quickly as you can while not emptying your hand.



NOTE: I prefer to cast Jihad covering two of my opponent's sites and two of my own, so that I can summon non-charge minions and still receive the +1 power benefit.



The Great Famine very specifically removes the strongest minion in a four-square area at the end of your turn. Very often, the minions in this deck are less powerful than the average minion my opponent is wanting to cast. You can survive a turn or two under its protection and force your opponent to forego summoning in order to wait out your aura's duration. This is also our answer when someone has a big problem underneath of a site. This card also carries a very important word for our success in its text box: "occupying". This means that The Great Famine (and also Lava Flow!) can remove threats that are burrowed or submerged. So if you're struggling to remove anything from a Root Spider to a Great Old One with confidence, this is your huckleberry.



Dangers in the Meta:


Pebbled Paths, Bottomless Pit, Perilous Bridge, Troll Bridge, Gnome Hollows and Impenetrable Copse. Use your Sinkholes or Smokestacks of Gnaak in a center position to make sure you can negate these nasty sites.


Archimago. I don't know what to tell you. You will lose sometimes to someone who can cast Divine Healing 6 times during a game and then Craterize you twice. Get them to deaths door asap so that they can't benefit from healing.


Enchantress. I don't know about this one really, I'm just very afraid of how this avatar completely flips the physics of the board state. Control tends to trump aggro in these games. Speed is your best friend.


Water players or Steam Druids with Polar Explorers and Ruler of Thul. It's very hard to rush forward when you have to watch your back. I recommend sticking to the game plan and holding on to some AoE fire spells and Monstrous lions to deal with whoever decides to come in the back door with bad intentions.




IMPORTANT NOTE:


You're going to take damage during this game. Don't get me wrong, lots of time you'll be playing way ahead of slower decks. But I also won a lot of games in this tournament on double-death's door. Try to keep your cool. You've usually got more damage in hand than your opponent. Stay vigilant and trust that you can win. Stay ahead by a turn. Get your opponent to door first and use fire to finish it. Don't worry about the score, just the result.


One game, I went down to door when my opponent (another fast air/earth Druid) still had 12 life. I was so disheartened and I was sure my day was over. But he had played all of his cards that could deal damage to my Druid, which was safely nestled on my back row. I was able to infiltrate his Pudge Butcher and leave it ineffective while I flooded the board with spells from my hand. I still had 3 or 4 spells in hand and I had 6 sites down so I could drop two spells a turn to put the pressure back on him. It was a close one, and the high-heart-rate monitor on my watch went off twice. But I came back and won it.


Another game, an opponent stole my Infernal Legion using Infiltrate, then played a Grim Guisarme and Warp Spasm the next turn to hit me for 24 with it. Before this play, though, the score had been 20-2 in my favor. The Legion died and he had played all of his cards. I was able to stabilize and win in two turns.


In the finals of the Crossroads tournament final, I was down 18-2. And the 2 damage he had taken, he did to himself. Talk about a blowout. I managed the win because I stayed the course and made the best, most efficient plays. Eventually, I cleared his board and played enough threats of my own to deal two big swings and get to double death's door. The deck has your back. Trust it, and trust that no game is over until it's over.


Conclusion:


You have one job. Burn. Do not spend time entertaining or even considering your opponent's intentions, actions or feelings.


Just. Do. Damage.


Quickly and consistently lower their life total while leaving yourself some spells in hand as options for future plays.


If you want to play with feelings, play with water. If you want to play with finesse, play with air. If you want to play with muscle, play with earth. But if you want to leave your enemy in ashes, play with fire!


;0)


I hope that you enjoy playing this deck and your own variations. Please let me know how it goes for you when you try it? Looking forward to hearing from you and seeing you at an event sometime soon!



-UnderSietch

deckinfo.name: Seeing Red - 1st place SCG Con Baltimore and NYC Cornerstone 2025
deckinfo.primer:
Seeing Red

Primer by UnderSietch


*UPDATE*


I’ve updated this decklist to reflect the one I played in the SCG CON Baltimore 2025, where I took 1st place. I've also update the primer for the new list and added more specific examples of how I play special cards, artifacts and auras in addition to the turn by turn card flow breakdown. Thank you for your interest and your feedback!


*NEW* Video of the Quarter Finals Match from SCG Con in Baltimore 2025 vs Count Tolstoy


Feature article on Sorcery TCG about Seeing Red and it's pilot, yours truly!


Video of the Championship Match at SCG CON in Baltimore 2025


Interview on Common Sense Sorcery Podcast about my win at SCG CON Baltimore


Team Covenant play-tests this deck on their YouTube channel ahead of SCG CON Houston! (gameplay at 50 mins)


Check out the video of the final match of the NYC King of the Realm cornerstone!


Introduction:


I'm typically a very whimsical deck builder. I like the story and the artwork and the intricate interactions between the weirdest and coolest cards. I often even write a little bit of lore to explain the narrative of the "characters" in my deck and how they came together to do battle against strange and ominous enemies. What can I say? I'm a nerd.


But with the tournament season approaching, I've been noticing an uptick in a more competitive and aggressive play-style all around me. This deck is a response to getting my butt relentlessly kicked over and over by some very good players and deck builders in my local community, who were tuning their tournament decks at our casual meetups. The calculated and efficient competition deck is a new adventure and mindset for me. And I think a good amount of beginners luck, mixed with being thrown to the wolves (sometimes literally) again and again, led to my winning our NYC cornerstone recently. I had been so tilted, so often, that I was literally SEEING RED.


Philosophy:


I decided that I wanted to make my games as short and sweet as possible. I don't want to allow other decks to get set up and start to hit me with big, intricate plays. My goal is to get my opponent in a reactive space, having to spend their precious few actions each game removing my threats and adapting to my board position, rather than imposing their will.


Playstyle:


I chose Mono-Fire because it's a fast and nasty suit. There are plenty of places to find extra damage for removal and to lower my opponents life total, while leaving me in an advantageous board-state. And it's very low cost!


I chose the Druid as my avatar for one reason: An immortal, airborne spellcaster, TAWNY. Flying around and dealing Fire's unblockable Area of Effect (AoE) damage to both remove enemy threats and deal damage to enemy avatars simultaneously.


The basic idea behind the deck is to combine the sometimes self-destructing damage from tawny, and genesis damage from deserts, with genesis and end-of-turn bonus damage from fire minion cards to remove enemy threats and deal damage without spending mana or losing my minions in a fight.


For example:


Opponent plays an Autumn Unicorn on turn 3.

I attack it with Tawny (she dies, but there's one damage), I play a desert (one damage and summon Tawny again, she's back!), and I play a vile imp for 2 mana and the genesis damage removes the Unicorn and leaves my Imp and Tawny alive. The board now has two threats on it for me and none for them.


Tawny's bonus damage also works in the reverse. You can cast an AoE spell, then attack with Tawny to deal one damage to an enemy minion THEN cast a desert to deal one additional damage and summon Tawny again for no cost.


For example:


Opponent drops a Atlas Wanderers on turn 4 due to a Mana boost from a Gothic Tower.

I cast Firebolts with Tawny, then attack the Atlas Wanderers with Tawny dealing a 4th damage, then I tap my Druid to play a Desert nearby, dealing the Atlas Wanderers a 5th and fatal damage and summoning Tawny again for no cost.


This allows me to destroy my opponents 5-cost drop with a total expenditure of 2 mana.


The last and most important note I'll make about our magical owl friend is that she's actually the perfect foil to your Druid opponents. By using a Torshammar Trinket, you can still have Tawny fly around near your opponent's avatar when they are Flipped and Bruin is active. Now that she's a 2 power, she can take steps nearby your opponents Druid and not die from their special ability. Then, she can cast a kill spell.


Use your owl. Give it a Torshammar Trinket and hit your opponents sites as often as possible. Cast Boudicca and give Tawny a Trinket and hit your opponent's sites with your owl for 5 damage. Be very active and rude with your bird friend. If your opponent is spending cards and mana removing your owl, you are winning. They are spending time, energy and resource on something that you get for free. Try your best to get them to react to your owl.


For me? The Bruin is a "smash in case of emergency" card. I want to spend most games not needing it. I want to be able to cast tawny by playing a site all game long. She's that important.



How and when to play:


You need to be patient!

(read that again)


This deck allows you to win FAST. I've observed that, in many games, Sorcery players cast anywhere from 12-18 spells and it can take up to 50 minutes to finish. In my games, my opponents cast 7-10 spells and the game can be over in 25 minutes.


(Which resulted in a very nice long break between rounds for me at the tournaments)


That doesn't mean that you play all of your cards out fast, however. Quite the contrary. It means you need to make every point of damage count. Hit their sites and Avatars early and as often as possible, yes. BUT DO NOT EMPTY YOUR HAND. You are leading the action while tactically responding to their drops. Find ways to remove their drop and increase your board presence AND deal them a little damage each turn. It's very possible. But you are most likely playing only one spell per turn. Your owl, deserts, genesis effects and end of turn effects will make it feel like you're doing much more than that but you're not. It's very simple and very deadly. And you'll need spells in your hand if your opponent manages to slow the game down and draw things out.



Turn by turn:


Mulligan:


You want a removal or control spell like Disintegrate, Immolation or Infiltrate in your hand ideally, and at least one cheap minion and one fire damage spell. Having three minions isn't the end of the world. You can have a War Horse, Colicky Dragonettes and Saracen Raiders and play forward from a really good place. The removal and fire magics will show up when you need them.


Make sure you have a Forge and at least one Desert in your hand, trust me. If you can't do that, make sure you have two fire threshold in your opening hand. Sinkholes and Wizard's Dens are awesome, don't mulligan them unless you have multiples in hand.


Ideal sample hand:


Disintegrate, War Horse, Minor Explosion

Forge, Red Desert, Poison Well



Turn by turn breakdown:


Turn 1: play the forge, make the lance, create Tawny and have her pick up the lance.


Turn 2: If you went first, Play a Bonfire or a Funeral Pyre or something forward toward your opponent and drop the War Horse and step Tawny forward to hand the lance off to your other minion. You don't always get the charge or genesis effects of minions and sites to land, that doesn't mean it's a bad play. Remember you're increasing your board presence with each drop and they'll have to spend resources to clear those spells, which you'll replace with more powerful ones as you draw them. Of course the best sites to play forward in a central position would be a Sinkhole, Smokestacks or Vesuvius. But we can't always get what we want.


If you went second, try dropping that Poisoned Well and get a hit on their life total, if they played forward toward you. Or play a Sinkhole forward to prepare for any unwanted sites. Wizard's Den is also a fantastic starting site, or a drop on turn three on your back row to get the extra spell draw.


Going second also means you can bring the lance up from Tawny, hand it off to the War Horse and immediately step forward to deal 3 first-strike damage to either a minion or, ideally, your opponent's site.


NOTE: You will draw spells and play the sites from your hand on the first three turns.


Turn 3: I love the Redcap Powries here, or even a Trinket on Tawny and Firebolts for removal or direct damage to the enemy avatar (that's 5 damage turn 3). When in doubt, Minor Explosion is the best, most effective card in this deck. I honestly have considered adding a 4th copy recently. Explode everything all of the time. Do not hesitate to do damage. It's your whole job. Do it often. Colicky Dragonettes are good here. Save your Kobolds for later unless there's an obvious play that maximizes their end of turn strike ability.



Turn 4: You will draw and play a site. This leaves you with four sites on the board and three or four spells in hand. Great cards open up on this turn: Saracen Raiders is an awesome free 3 damage on an unprotected and unsuspecting opponent's site. Infiltrate becomes an option, but I typically save this until my opponent drops something that seems like a game-changing bomb. Think Pudge Butcher or Seirawan Hydra. These are the things you want to take and tap down and keep them out of the game. Redcap Powries with a Torshammer Trinket is a favorite of mine to remove a 4 power minion or strike a site for 4. Boudicca opens up on Turn 4, but don't drop her on the board unless Tawny and/or another minion can undoubtedly strike a site freely. Her ability is too good to waste. If you play Boudicca back and away from the fray, you may get multiple turns with her ability in play and swing the game heavily in your favor.



Turn 5: draw a spell and tap to draw a site. The only reason you would draw a site to play here is if you already have Rebecks in your hand and you see a good opportunity to use your charge giant to get a big hit in on your opponent. Otherwise, stick to the plan so you can have 5 sites next turn.


Turn 6: Draw a spell and play your 5th site. This should leave you with 3 or 4 spells in hand and five sites on the board. You can play everything in the deck besides Infernal Legion with this board state. This is where the world opens up to you. Try to spread your minions out as much as possible so that they're more difficult to remove. Your opponent is going to scratch and claw to stabilize. There may be temptation at times to play multiple cards from your own hand. Only do this if it lands your opponent at death's door or decisively swings the game toward your win.


Turn 7: Draw a spell and tap to draw a site. Now you have all of the sites that you'll ever need and you have three or 4 spells in hand. This is what I mean by BE PATIENT. You'll find yourself in a remarkable board state with plenty of spells in hand. If you can leverage your extra damage well, you might still have two or three threats on the board at this point.



How to Deal Damage:


Every time that you can, play a minion with charge and hit your opponent's sites. Every time that you can, cast fire spells that hit their avatar or groups of minions. By turn 5 or 6, you may have taken half of their life total away by chipping away with Tawny, fire damage and minions hitting sites.


I usually find that I'm holding more immediate damage threats than my opponent. If I consistently am hitting them once per turn for 3+ damage, I get them a little off their game and they start to have to waste resources and dig for answers.


Try not to win more. Win just enough. You really want those three spells in hand to deal with some of the game's inherent big swings.


How to win:


You didn't flip your Druid, did you? Good. Being able to summon Tawny (and maybe put a Trinket on her) and get her into position to deal a Minor Explosion, Firebreathing, Lava Flow, Firebolts or Firebreathing is your ticket to victory. Good players keep a kill in their hand when they can. If you can hold onto one of these spells and not use it until you get your opponent to death's door, you'll have a tidy and efficient victory on your hands.


Remove their threats when they're on death's door. Get rid of their minions, and clear your path. Sometimes you don't have the fire spell and you need superior numbers of minions to get a strike in. Don't forget to remove their blockers to make a charge minion very deadly.


Sometimes, walking your druid forward and then flipping for Bruin and your special ability, can pin their Avatar down when it's on deaths door and keep it from being able to run away from your fire damage. In this case only, you don't need Tawny, because your Avatar is your spellcaster.



Special cards and their uses:


Your damage (most of it) comes from your small minions and fire spells from Tawny. But sometimes you need to be able to flex into a more midrange role and become a bigger beast to seal the deal against a powerful opponent.


There are a few HUGE drops in this deck that help you out a lot.


Rebecks is my favorite card here, dealing 4 damage to an opponent's site on the same turn that you play it. Pair him with a Torshammer Trinket or Jihad for a bigger swing. Have him ride a warhorse to get him into a deeper and more problematic position for an opponent. On a later turn, use a fire spell to clear out a blocker before dropping Rebecks to get a free hit on your opponent's site.


Boudicca on turn 4 when you have Tawny and maybe a War Horse and a Redcap Powries on the board? Do some math here, that's 15 damage if they all go unblocked to your opponent's sites. Normally I play her very carefully away from the battle. But sometimes she can create a very welcome distraction. While your opponent focuses on removing her, you can keep hitting for 2-5 damage per turn on their life total. Remember the goal is to get them to door and ping them for the win. If you lose cards and life along the way, so be it. Don't win more! Just win. Never waste resources to save a special card.


Siege Giants are amazing. These guys are why I don't have to play Blaze or Mad Dash in this deck. I get all of the movement I need from these dudes. They can throw 21 of the cards in this deck (including Avatar and Tawny), to any nearby site without having to tap for the ability. They can even throw a War Horse that they themselves are riding. READ THAT AGAIN. They can saddle up on a horse, throw that horse diagonally, then both the horse and the giant still can take a step and declare an attack. Use Siege Giant to spread your damage out far and wide, like a joyful flaming trebuchet.


Monstrous Lion's job is actually as a removal spell. I use it to deal a surprise and tidy four damage to an enemy that's on my border or in my territory. Sometimes a BattleMage or some other antsy Avatar gets too close and catches a lion to the face. Don't expect the Lion to live for more than one turn very often. Add a Torshammer Trinket on turn 5 or later for extra Lion.


Askelon Phoenix is in the deck to provide air support and fire resistance. You'll very rarely use its ability to power it up. But it takes no damage from fire spells, minions or abilities. It survives a poison nova. Heck, it survives a direct strike from Ignis Rex holding Crown of the Victor. It's a good card, and is usually a sort of turret or defensive/support play for me, more so than a beatdown.

hint.name: Shapeshift 2nd place SCG-Baltimore
hint.primer:
Hello all! Thanks for checking out my pet deck, Shapeshift!

This primer is a work in progress.


This deck is a bit of a pet deck of mine. It started off as a way to see if I could make big water monsters a viable strategy back when the meta was aggro and magoo. It was always fun but wasn't always all that viable.


Then with the rules change aggro and Archimago got a bit weaker and midrange was back in vogue. My good buddy Pascal (fuenfrappe on discord and 2nd place at Gencon!!!)?told me I should bring this to Gencon. I started testing and tweaking and it turns out Pascal was right. This deck was more than viable!


As a result this deck had now won me 2 rainbow foil druids and is the most fun deck I've played in the current meta. I hope you enjoy!


The gameplan:


This deck requires a lot of knowledge about the game but apart from positioning and maximizing card potential it's a pretty straightforward deck. Basically I've got all the good cards for 4+ mana and just need to get there. The early game is just stall and buy time, then the late game is present threat after threat after threat and out value your opponent. You can win with just about any minion in the deck.




The deck:


I'll try to go through each card and why they are here, I'll also post a video on my YouTube channel If you prefer the visual reference.


The Auras:

These are self explanatory. Atlantean fate is one of the best cards in the game. It wipes the opponents board, submerges their artifacts, kills their spiders, and ruins their threshold. Not a whole lot to explain here other than in the current meta with so much water running around people are running a lot more ordinary sites to nerf this card specifically. One thing to remember is to throw water sites on your front row so if you need an emergency fate in your own sites you don't lose threshold when drowning their minions.


Black plague is just hard removal. Kills just about anything if you position it right and it should already gain you value by the time they can dispel it if they are inclined to. Against aggressive creature based decks, if they take a turn off from playing creatures to get rid of the plague, I'll throw my grandmaster wizards or tawney into the black plague just to keep it around and buy more time.


The artifacts:


Ring is self explanatory. It's the most ubiquetous and busted card in the game. I don't really need it early against most opponents but it's fantastic early against AoA and aggro decks. Ring, trinket, and tawney, can dismantle aggro decks on their own. You don't even need another spells. The one thing to mention is don't play it out til you're ready to use it bc between dispel, drown; bury, disenchant, swap, shatter strike.... It's a card every deck is packing removal for


Trinkets: yeahhhhh these are busted with tawney. Getting one means you're pushing real damage with tawney from the start, getting two Means tawney is trading for any aggro minion, getting 3 feels unfair. Lookout lugbog cat, my 4 power flyer doesn't even cost me a card. I will always keep a trinket in my opening hand. Depending on the matchup I might keep 3 (don't do this agaisnt fire based decks. If you don't know what your opponent is on don't keep 3 trinkets. If they have deserts you're just not playing the game lol) this is safe into AoA, AoE, waveshaper, deathspeaker etc.

As a result this deck had now won me 2 rainbow foil druids and is the most fun deck I've played in the current meta. I hope you enjoy!


The gameplan:


This deck requires a lot of knowledge about the game but apart from positioning and maximizing card potential it's a pretty straightforward deck. Basically I've got all the good cards for 4+ mana and just need to get there. The early game is just stall and buy time, then the late game is present threat after threat after threat and out value your opponent. You can win with just about any minion in the deck.




The deck:


I'll try to go through each card and why they are here, I'll also post a video on my YouTube channel If you prefer the visual reference.


The Auras:

These are self explanatory. Atlantean fate is one of the best cards in the game. It wipes the opponents board, submerges their artifacts, kills their spiders, and ruins their threshold. Not a whole lot to explain here other than in the current meta with so much water running around people are running a lot more ordinary sites to nerf this card specifically. One thing to remember is to throw water sites on your front row so if you need an emergency fate in your own sites you don't lose threshold when drowning their minions.


Black plague is just hard removal. Kills just about anything if you position it right and it should already gain you value by the time they can dispel it if they are inclined to. Against aggressive creature based decks, if they take a turn off from playing creatures to get rid of the plague, I'll throw my grandmaster wizards or tawney into the black plague just to keep it around and buy more time.


The artifacts:


Ring is self explanatory. It's the most ubiquetous and busted card in the game. I don't really need it early against most opponents but it's fantastic early against AoA and aggro decks. Ring, trinket, and tawney, can dismantle aggro decks on their own. You don't even need another spells. The one thing to mention is don't play it out til you're ready to use it bc between dispel, drown; bury, disenchant, swap, shatter strike.... It's a card every deck is packing removal for


Trinkets: yeahhhhh these are busted with tawney. Getting one means you're pushing real damage with tawney from the start, getting two Means tawney is trading for any aggro minion, getting 3 feels unfair. Lookout lugbog cat, my 4 power flyer doesn't even cost me a card. I will always keep a trinket in my opening hand. Depending on the matchup I might keep 3 (don't do this agaisnt fire based decks. If you don't know what your opponent is on don't keep 3 trinkets. If they have deserts you're just not playing the game lol) this is safe into AoA, AoE, waveshaper, deathspeaker etc.

hint.name: SCGcon Baltimore Top 8 (7-0 Swiss)
hint.primer:
Slightly greedy steam druid splash for air. Steam + Air.


Font of life is swap.


Went 7-0 in swiss then lost immediately in top cut. Fantastic tournament and community. Everyone was awesome. I'm coming back for the rainbow foil next time.


Won 6/7 druid semi-mirrors. Felt very good all day, don't have changes at the moment except maybe adjusting more for the bigger water based druid lists. Felt like I could use a little more consistency in racing so I could push the early game advantage against the big water decks. CJ's list and the Melbourne list felt real rough.


Everything else (Water air battle mage, fire air druid, air druid, earth water air druid, 2 steam druids) went exactly as I had hoped. Trade efficiently early, turn the corner, close quickly with unique-slop shenanigans.


Main recommendation if you want to try this deck is to mulligan to early game curve spells + removal, bottom uniques and late game unless it's your best card in the matchup by a lot. And then draw a site for turn early at least once on any turn where you have a clear play in hand. Even on your first draw of the game. Very important to be able to space your sites based on the most info you can to get the most out of the early game tempo. I see a lot of druids refuse to draw a spell for turn for value reasons. But this deck wants to go a little bigger and play carefully around site distruction and flood based decks.

hint.primer:
Deck is meant to play well into [[Druid]]. The idea for this tournament was to win the first 2-3 games and get paired up against multiple [[Druid]] at the top tables.


Why no Earth? Earth was cut in order to play cards that are good specifically against [[Druid]]. Sites such as [[Arid Desert]], [[Red Desert]], and [[Remote Desert]] are very strong against [[Druid]]'s Tawny. Powerful three threshold Air spells [[Browse]] and [[Arcane Barrage]] are very good but unable to be played in a three color deck. Same rationale for the inclusion of [[Merlin's Tower]], [[Wizard's Den]], and more Towers [[Dark Tower]], [[Gothic Tower]], and [[Lone Tower]]. Although you lose [[Land Surveyor]], [[Earthquake]], and [[Common Sense]], cards like [[Clamor of Harpies]], 3x [[Poison Nova]], as well as [[The Black Plague]], and [[The Great Famine]] allow you to slow the game down even if your opponent is playing Water. This list was ultimately experimental and it did surprisingly well without any playtesting.


Win conditions: [[Nimbus Jinn]] combo or repeated big magic spells ([[Major Explosion]] and [[Arcane Barrage]])

deckinfo.name: Archimago Control
deckinfo.primer:
Deck tier: S

Deck Difficulty: S

Counters: N/A

Does it beat roots though? Yes it does in 40-20 (list in link)

How is this list currently configured? All rounder - mostly ideal for bo1. See meta section and side/maybe board for ideas on how to build your deck if a tournament finally runs bo3.



Matchups:


SORCERER - GENERALLY GOOD


Sorc (air fire) - 6/4 - You lose to uniques or drawing poorly mostly. The average game goes long and it's whoever draws their good stuff first which is likely you. Managing sites is the most important part of this matchup.

Sorc(earth fire) - 7/3 - Free food. You die to uniques. Don't be dumb about site placement and be smart about where you position your avatar.

Sorc(water fire) 6/4 - They have slower but more bursty turns which is painful. Be smart about what you let live to be greedy. Be smart about atlantean fate and ruler.


PF - GENERALLY GOOD

Generally, this will be an attrition war between turns 3-10. You will pull ahead on average but the games they draw more of their wizards or must answers, utilizing your sweepers correctly is the way you win those games. Additionally, this is a matchup where I think it's ok to be boxed in if you can't reasonable defend all your sites and drawing action is likely more important than getting boxed in if they have a lot of movement.



PF (land destruction) 6/4 - In your favor. Understanding when to draw sites vs spells is most important in the matchups. Understanding how to play around bells is also required. From their perspective, its hard to draw both land destruction and meaningful pressure early so plan accordingly. Try not to give them sites near your avatar and use blink to facilitate that midgame. Difficult matchup if you don't know what you are doing.


PF midrange - 7/3 - Free food. funnel their minions. Don't bother cutting them off its just more things you need to defend. You lose to craterize / big minion turn but you are more likely to draw your big action first.


PF Aggro 5/5 - Difficult matchup to pilot well. If you don't draw your early spiders and defensive sites, it's extremely hard to keep up with removal because of the nature of avatar. PF opens up your sites to be more vulnerable by playing everywhere. Mulligan aggressively for spiders/ kettletop/defensive sites/egg.



DRUID - GENERALLY REALLY GOOD.


Druid midrange - 6/4- Incidental damage from tawny is your downfall if you don't manage it well. You lose by them highrolling their uniques or drawing poorly. Don't mismanage your sweepers.


Druid spirits - 6/4 - Charge is scary because its behind your defensive sites and it gets around pebbled path. You lose by drawing poorly or mismanaging your avatar into big door turns from jhin / big minion + grapple.


Druid control - 9/1 - I'm not sure how you lose this matchup.


Druid aggro - 8/2 - Free food. Less scary than sorcerer. It's ok to throw spells away for tempo because they don't have inherent means to card advantage. Spider is an allstar against them.


FLAME CALLER - GENERALLY EQUAL

Expect rift valley/pyres and plan accordingly.


Flame caller (air/fire) - 6/4 - This matchup is really about getting your big beefy minions after you stabilize. Try to force them to burn their tap ability on your big minions. Mulligans for sites are most important in this matchup in pebbled path/perilous bridge/pyre etc. Try not to board wipe them without considering your health and charge + tap from them. Managing their creatures with sites/spiders is key. Try to hold onto pyre/pillar for board wipes so you don't immediately die to blink+tap. There are god hands they can have and there are extremely brutal hands you can have. See mulligan section


Flame caller(mono fire) 7/3 - Worse than the air variant. The plan is the same but the speed is slower.


Elementalist - GENERALLY FREE


Ele Water control - 8/2 - Don't get leviathan'd. Half their deck is dead to you, just loop spells until you find craterize. Also don't be stupid about atlantean fate.

Ele burn control - 9/1 - It's a craterize war where you see 3x more of your deck

Ele midrange - 8/2 - Same gameplan against other creature decks. Just don't get jhined and funnel creatures with sites/spider. be careful of geyser if you are holding a large amount of power with one spider.


DEATHSPEAKER - EVEN/LOSSES


DS Jhin control - 5-5. Expect them to have a means to move you out of gnome hollows. You lose by playing sites/spiders poorly or mismanaging their creatures/graveyard. Knowing when to remove minions is key. It's an attrition war where you both see your deck by the time someone dies and both parties have yard hate. Egg is an all star in this matchup. Dont feed them your morgana or wizard. If you are on a greedier list with feast this matchup is significantly better.


ENCHANTRESS - Slightly good to even


Ench Control - 7/3 - Don't just play spiders into nothing. Undertanding your role is important in this matchup. Sometimes you just have 5 bolts and you can swing on their sites with your avatar. Half their deck is bad against you. Don't be stupid about your site placement in your back row.


Ench aggro(fire air) - 6/4 - Prioritize finding means of lifegain and spider. Your auras kill one thing then die against them so use them as such. Manage their burn auras with blink in the midgame if you don't have disenchant/dispel. Kettletop is good pressure when the board develops and can be used as bait to draw out damage auras. Site placement is key so they dont get double hits on you with things like spin attack.


Ench midrange (fire water) - 5/5 - Matchup is way better sideboarded. Prioritize life gain, threshold sites(not defensive), and kettletop in mulligans. Site placement is key or you will die to double hits from auras before you can heal. Play your vampires on your home site or somewhere the auras cant animate so you dont lose them to strike effects. Vampires, titan, and craterize are the things you are digging for with browse/cantrips in the mid game. Save disenchant / bury effects for wild fire because it gets past your site placement for strike effects on top of you.



just a reminder, site placement against enchantress for everyone:


site site site site site

site site site


Templar - 9-1 - Absolutely free


AOA - GENERALLY FREE. All versions come down to drawing healing or spiders. (7/3)


Avatar of Earth - Generally Good


DONT GET RIFT VALLEYED ON TURN TWO. ON THE PLAY, PLAY SIDEWAYS AS SECOND SITE. It's mostly a race for damage/damage mitigation. Use lifegain to offset their attacks while you yourself attack with your minions / bolts once they try to get on top of you unless you see good craterize opportunities. Understanding your role in the board state is crucial. Common sense for kettletop is extremely strong to pressure them. Leverage your life for your creatures and race them down when you feel comfortable instead of blocking most of the time.


AOE (E/F) - 6/4 - well timed pyres hurt. Their deck mostly sucks against you but it comes down to chumpers and understanding your role in the matchup. Because they will be on top of you at variable time, knowing if you are on craterize plan or not is important. If they have 5 sites or less, then craterize becomes a timewalk even if you dont damage them but honestly i usually race them with my other burn spells and attack their sites eventually with my avatar at 7 mana. Hard to pilot but it is heavily favored if you know what you are doing. This matchup can easily be teched into as well which would make it a 7/3 matchup.


AOE(E/A) - 7/3 - Generally free - The lack of incidental damage from charge is noticable. Same as above, use defensive sites to slow them down. Be smart about their earthquakes getting value and rift valley as their second site.



Battlemage - Generally Good

This matchup gets incredibly better if you prepare for it. Craterize is dead mostly, prepare to attack with minions and your avatar. Understanding your role based on your cards is crucially important. The best means of using craterize is prepositioning towards their sites away from center line and walking/blink away to blow up their site + damage to them because they will want to stay on top of you to minimize craterize impact.


BM (W/A) - 6/4 - Your defensive sites are some bullshit for them. Sit in a gnome hollow. They win when you fail to draw healing or not meaningfully stalling them with sites. Throw away all your mid/late game spells because you lose to tempo not CA. Gnome hollow as your first site and playing your second site sideways is really strong.


BM (A/F) - 5/5 - Same thing, your site are nuts against them. Sitting in gnome doesnt help against shatter strike. Be smart about where you play your egg (not in your hands).


Mirror - ???

This matchup is about who gets their toys first or answers to said toys. Kettletop is great in this matchup because bolts at them are not bolts at you or they pressure their life total over time.


Archi control - 5/5 - Whoever craterizes first usually wins. Aggressively mul for your win conditions and merlins tower. If you don't have it setup by turn 6, use your blinks to move onto their sites without sacrificing your tap to draw site ability ideally. Even if your opponent is spamming a bunch of cards, its not actually much card advantage so keep that in mind. I'd rather have craterize locked and loaded than having to dig because in the mirror, you are using your yard to dig harder towards your win conditions anyway. The player who doesn't get their win condition can win by attacking/bolting pretty easily especially if you manage to draw ring and closed the distance as suggested above.


Feast targets: early - craterize, arcane barrage. midgame (when you have craterize first) - divine healing, lightning bolt. midgame (when you dont have craterize) - craterize, divine healing.


Archi tokens - 6/4 - Watchout for boudica/gigantism. Same stuff as above but they have less means to dig through their deck. Save novas for their big turns.


Mulligans:


Against charge aggro - Mulligan for sites and early removal/minions. bolts/kettletop/spiders are MVPS

Against spirit aggro - Mulligan for gnome hollows, spiders, and 5 mana board wipes

Against the mirror - Mulligan for cyclers, acceleration sites, kettletop, and prioritize finding craterize. Your best site to find is merlins tower so you can craterize on turn 5.

Against midrange - Mulligan for sweepers, common sense, and plague/famine.

Against flame caller - Mulligan for early removal/spider/egg and pyre/pillar/defensive sites. Spider, pyre/pilar, and egg are the priority.

Against PF - Mulligan for common sense, kettletop, morgana, and grandmaster wizard. This is generally an attrition war where you need to also be wary of turns 1-4 because you can't prioritize mulls for sites. If you naturally have defensive sites then you are set.

Against BM/AOE - Mull for divine healing and defensive sites.

Against sparkmage - Mull for egg/divine healing/kettletop/princess


How to prepare for specific Meta


Lots of charge aggro? Consider running vampire, holy ground, and more bolts. Guards as a potential substitute for explosion. cut infiltrate. cut death dealer.

Anti agro magoo - https://curiosa.io/decks/cm7tlhufq0021jy03i373gle6


Lots of midrange? Use this list or a more token oriented approach if you don't like direct damage. This list is tuned to be well rounded but take a slight loss to aggro.


Lots of avatars that attack themselves? Cut craterize and run 2x wraetanis titan, 1 grapple, 1/2 arcane barrage or guards, and vampire. Consider cutting famine/plague or other non damage removal as well. Make sure you have 3x quagmire.


Lots of the mirror? The greedier the better. merlin, feast, orb of bal, and rescue. Cut 1-2 novas. Consider dropping fire for more cyclers. Consider dropping the auras. Consider sisters of avalon if the meta is otherwise aggro.


Lots of burrow minions? add lava but this is largely unnecessary


Lots of burn? Consider holy ground and vampires. cut death dealer, morg, and valley+river of flame. Cut plague/famine.



How do you play this deck well?

0) Understanding when you are strong and when you are vulnerable.

1) Understanding damage breakpoints your opponents deck has and being able to anticipate damage accurately.

2) Leveraging your life for card advantage at safe points (see 1). IE: Common sense loop and when to do a bunch or just one for one. I generally tend to do just 2 so that i can recast the thing i get from common sense.

3) Understanding your role in board states. I attack with my avatar surprisingly a lot especially in the mirror and against AOE.

4) Mulligan well.

5) Leveraging your spells well. This deck is incredibly hard to play at the top level because you don't actually have much inherent card advantage but what you do have is incredible card quality and the ability to rebuy those cards. General rule of thumb is if you don't have a good defensive site or means to interact with your opponent, don't play your second site forward. On the play against something that you suspect has rift valley, don't play forward for your second site.

8) using your blinks to preposition in lots of matchups. IE: getting out of grapple line of sight or forward for nova against midrange/aggro

9) creative uses of your spells and sites. IE: EQ to ruin tri sites


Addressing common misconceptions about the deck

1) Your ability doesn't inherently draw you a lot of cards. It's 1/3 a card per spell you play.

2) It's far from unbeatable. It's matchup spread is just great which is what makes it dumb. One small mistake will easily cost you the game.

3) It's a control deck and while it's an S tier deck, that doesn't mean matchups are as free as people make it seem. Inherently, it requires deep understanding of your opponents deck and all playlines your deck has. IE: Getting max value from philostone when you have multiple casters. The skill floor is low but the skill ceiling is insanely high for the avatar. Easily the hardest avatar in the game to master at the moment. (no, enchantress isnt hard to master, thats a meme from alpha honestly. Enchantress was and is largely just a rules knowledge check for both players but one dimensionally so)

4) The utility creatures don't do anything if you build your deck correctly. They can be problematic if they are all played on the same turn but all of them die various cards in the deck. Salt boy? nearly everything. Worry wart? twister to void, infiltrate, bury, deathdealer, plague/famine, blink + punch. Burrow stuff? plague / famine, death dealer, river of flame + any fire spell, merlins tower + any removal underneath.

5) water isn't a great counter but its good in bo1 as your bury effects are dead until they attack but thats only 3 pieces of removal in this list.


FAQ

1) Why not tris? They make you vulnerable to earthquake and lose you some % of games

2) Why annual fair? Allows you to play 3 pip spells of multiple colors without the need for tris and is extremely clutch when your sites are being destroyed.

3) Why 3 colors instead of two? Fire solves a significant portion of problems earth/air could have and abuse philo stone harder. Earth Fire lacks some amount of card quality compared to earth air. Annual fair solves threshold issues anyways.

4) Why are there so many one ofs? At the top end, you don't want to put all your eggs into just craterize because of feast. The other one ofs are just redundant effects I want or common sense targets.

5) What happened to sisters of avalon? Just circumstance of what I expected to go up against. Below are my thoughts on when to use it.

-Put sisters in your deck when the meta is fast and you have a lot of top end cards. You don't win through card advantage but card quality anyway. This gives a blocker, free positioning for nova, and throws expensive top end cards in harsh aggro matchups (or dead cards).

6) When kettletop? It mostly reads, gain 3-4 life and draw a card. Against the mirror or other slower decks, it can easily get in there for 2-6 damage because they don't want you the card. Have this in when the meta is really fast or is targetting your sites. Drop this card when the meta is really slow (likely not a thing).

7) What about water in the list? Thats a different deck(s). I'm sure someone will or has made content around it. Water is good though.

8) What does fire give? Means to deal with the subterrain, more sweepers, and funeral pyre for the mirror/flame caller

9) What does air give? Raw card advantage, defensive sites, the best movement/cycler in blink, accelerated mana, and browse.

10) What does earth give? Defensive sites, divine healing, root spider, and common sense. Notice i didnt mention craterize, every color has finishers it just so happens to be the best but not by a large margin unless you are doing orb. Honorable mention is kettleboy, he does work.

11) When should I play two color over three? When site destruction and generic charge aggro is all you play against. Holy grounds do work and not caringa bout a third color makes things easier.

12) What about bo3 or sideboards? This deck doesn't lose with sideboards and shines in best of 3.

deckinfo.name: BIRDS BIRDS BIRDS (1st Place League S4)
deckinfo.primer:
Intro 🌟

Hi everyone, I'm Kevin. This is the list that I created over the course of the 4th Discord league, eventually taking the win with in the top cut. Potato Knight also ran the list, coming 3rd/4th, so effectively it went 7-0, losing only to itself.


The list is basically aggro fliers with artifact support. You slap down as many bodies as you can, split them up to avoid Poison Novas and Earthquakes, then use your aerial advantage to strategically pick your opponent apart while presenting a solid defence with free cities and bottomless pits.


Lots of the cards here are already covered by other AoA lists, so I'll stick to explaining my modifications.


Card Explanations 📄

[[Plumed Pegasus]] / [[Haast Eagle]]

The namesake of the deck, our birds (Eagles are just Pegasus with worse threshold). It took me the longest time to figure these out (thanks Duo!) but really glad I tested them. Flying [[Bosk Trolls]] might not sound impressive at first, but I believe airborne is a massively underrated ability. In Sorcery, minions are removal. Airborne removes the ability for our opponent to attack back, creating a unilateral beatdown - we can still use our minions as removal, while theirs are stuck defending. Combine this with Trinkets and you end up with an extremely annoying suite of minions (can't be easily imp'd, kolbods'd, or attacked) that usually at best is 1-for-1'd by our opponent. The best part is, we don't really care! Their low cost and our minion density means we're usually deploying a new one every turn - embracing this 'throw minions at your opponents face until they door' is the core philosophy of this deck.


Devil's Eggs

These bad boys let you win games that I otherwise consider unwinnable, or extremely grindy at best. You have many ways to get this to an annoying place (bats, cloud spirits, AoA herself), and once it sticks, it creates an immense amount of pressure for your opponent - the clock is ticking. Also cancels out Angel's Eggs, which more decks are running now to our chagrin (if you ever find a way to steal them, make sure you do!).


Maddening Bells

Bells are often seen in control/tax decks, but I think it's one of the most powerful aggro cards. Combined with your mobility and towers, you can fairly frequently land a bells on your opponent by turn 3. On the play, I've had opponents concede immediately. While one of the worst cards you can draw late game, it has led to so many blow outs I still keep it, if for nothing else but the mind games.


Cloud Spirit

A really solid 2 power minion. Sadly rarely get to play it on curve due the threshold, but a card that's as good late game as it is early - a universal blocker/attacker is a massive headache for your opponents to play around.


Headless Haunt

I was on the fence for the longest time with these (what if they fall into the Bottomless Pits!?) but now I'm a believer. Lots of people think that the randomness is a downside - it really isn't, it's more of a weird form of evasion - and that 3 cost 4 body is amazing. Play this deep in the void and watch your opponent sweat figuring out how to block it.


Sinkhole

After I tried bells, I had the realization that this is exactly what the deck needed - a way to keep the game in 'early game' for as long as possible. Sinkholes not only acts as an amazing utility card (blow up the roots combo, get rid of their threshold etc.), but is most importantly free mana denial. While you vomit fliers onto the board, your opponents are stuck with an earthquake and 3 mana. One of the best cards in the game, never remove this.


Cut Cards ✂️

Skirmishers of Mu

One of the more controversial cuts, but after testing a bunch I've decided it's for the best. While the synergy with AoA is undeniable, for a 4 cost investment (your whole turn in this deck), Skirmishers are too easy to play around and remove for opponents that know what's coming. It's one of those cards that feel great when you get to trinket it, swing for 8, but then you forget all the times it dies to a lightning bolt, or a firebolts, or swings for 3 then dies to a unicorn, etc.


Phantasmal Shades

Just barely cut, could be in sideboard. 3 cost 4 power is amazing, but it's ability requires too much baby-sitting for our liking. One theme you will notice with our minions is that they're all very 'independent'. We spread them out like little missiles and then forget about them. This causes all sorts of headaches for our opponent and allows our Avatar to boulder, swing herself, defend the sites, etc.


Daperyll Vampires

Extremely powerful against mirror match, and aggro in general. Sadly too expensive, slow, and vulnerable for our deck (read above). A great sideboard card though, I'll have a minimum of 2 of these there.


Hounds of Ondaros

I really like these guys - they're a massive PITA to remove, so don't fall under the same umbrella as Mu/Vamps/Shades - they're about as resilient/independent as it gets. Unfortunately, they also do nothing for the first 5 turns of the game, and their upside is an evasive bird with +1 power for +2 cost...so they're a cut.


Spectral Stalker

Cute turn 1 tower play aside, these don't do much but die to imps/kobolds.


Browse

Another controversial cut - this is probably the best late game top-deck in the game. Unfortunately, there will be many games where this sits dead in your hand for the first 5 turns - we often have trouble hitting 3 x Air due to the neutral sites, and 1 mana is also non-trivial due to our super low curve.


Chain Lightning

Arguably the best finisher in the game - with AoA it's basically an guaranteed kill. Unfortunately outside of that one specific use-case, I found the card to be quite underwhelming - while it can be used for 4 mana to kill 2 small minions, you usually have much better uses of 4 mana. The 2 mana mode is terrible (bolts is much better), and you'll basically never do it with 6+.


Thunderstorm

Very matchup dependant card; I just found it too clunky to use. Haven't tested with this enough though, PK insists it's the best card since Poison Nova. 4 mana is just a lot, and our list is already very tight.


Credits 🎉

Potato Knight for all the help with playtesting, repping the deck, and being awesome in general!

Wulfinite, DarthNunu, MattdogNZ, and CJ for being top blokes and encouraging me through the league!

Duo for our chat that inspired my initial testing of Plumed Pegasus!

Jacksun and Drew from OnThePlay for the initial inspiration behind playing the deck!

All the cool peeps I met playing the game on discord - you know who you are!

My amazing gf for playtesting and moral support, and pulling my foil AoA 😁


Finally, shout out to all the people that helped run the league, it was my first foray into competitive Sorcery and you guys made it super fun. Cheers!

deckinfo.name: GenCon 2025 Crossroads - Mono Air (4th Place)
deckinfo.primer:
Intro 🌟

Hello all - my name is Joey. This is a list that I created and refined off of originally from the BIRDS BIRDS BIRDS (1st Place League S4) deck created by @Nvekmm which won season 4 of the TTS League. After playing a version of this deck at SorceryCon 2024 and missing out on the top cut (9th place, 5-2) due to getting blasted by two Archimagos, I decided to attempt a swing at a Mono Air deck that deviated more from the pure cheap minion aggro of BIRDS.


To be clear, relatively cheap airborne minions and the wildly flexible ability of the Avatar of Air are still the bread and butter of this deck, but it can now curve out into a mid-range game if neccesary. At Gen Con 2025, it went 6-1, beating 2 Druids, 2 Pathfinders, 1 Archimago, and 1 Enchantress. It only lost to a nasty Geomancer deck played by Ira.


Like BIRDS, the list is mostly aggro fliers with artifact support. You slap down as many bodies as you can, split them up to avoid Poison Novas and Earthquakes, then use your aerial advantage to strategically pick your opponent apart while slowing downthe enemy with defensive sites like Bottomless Pits, Sinkholes, Perilous Bridges, and even Bower of Bliss.


Below are some highlights of why certain cards made the cut:


Card Explanations 📄

Tooth Faeries

Potentially controversial, but I've never been big on Palliburrie Bats or their combo with Highland Falconer. Yeah, you can get two bodies on the board quick with 2 mana, but the 1 health non-airborne unit is too easily dealt with and doesn't jibe with the deck. Plus, the burrowing feature of the bats isn't very helpful now that I took out Devil's Eggs. Tooth Faeries have a special ability that - let's be honest - won't be helpful 80% of the time. However, it has won me games when I can prevent a chunky opposing minion from blocking at the start of my turn. Definitely a Bats upgrade in my opinion.


Cloud Spirit

An airborne 2 power minion that can effectively reach anywhere on the board. Especially in a game where the opponent has Gnome Hollows, they're amazing. Vastly underrated even in the midgame.


Headless Haunt

I was on the fence for the longest time with these (what if they fall into the Bottomless Pits!?) but now I'm a believer. Lots of people think that the randomness is a downside - it really isn't, it's more of a weird form of evasion - and that 3 cost 4 body is amazing. Play this deep in the void and watch your opponent sweat figuring out how to block it.


Daperyll Vampires

A must add with new rules noting that attacks on sites are strikes. Important for midrange beef.


Hounds of Ondaros

Very hard to remove 4 power minions. Again, important for midrange beef.


Castle Haunt

Getting too cute? Maybe. But these won me at least 2 games at the Gen Con Crossroads tourney. Still a 3 for 4 like Headless Haunt, but with the abiliy to be cast to your opponent's site directly. Worst case, I can usually cast him to one of my unique/elite sites for defense if my opponent has no sites to use. Yes, it's still risky, but IMO less risky than Headless Haunt.


Chain Lightning

An automatic finisher for only 2 mana with AoA's positioning ability. If in a rough spot, the ability to do 2-4 damage to a crowded minion field is also versatile.


Attack By Night

What's better than Disenchanting your opponent's artifacts? Taking them for yourself. Controversial within my local play group, but I believe this to be a versatile card that's worth a deeper look. Against an opponent who's artifact heavy (Battlemage, Archimago, Deathspeaker), you can force your opponent to drop all their items and then typically swoop in with your AoA's superior movement ability (or Cloud Spirit) to grab them. If you're not playing against an artifact heavy deck, the first strike for all your minions ability can be extremely helpful for clearing things out if you have plenty of minions on the board but the opponent is matching you.


Chaos Twister

Still the ultimate removal spell with upside. Just practice your blowing technique.


Mask of Mayhem / Grim Guisarme

With the rules change noting attacks on sites are strikes, Mask is a Godsend for decks with a lot of minions (of which, this is 60% minions). Be sure to not play it too early - typically only if you can take someone to door. Nothing like having a couple of Assassins come from the void to strike out of nowhere for 12 damage. Guisarme I am less convinced of in this deck - it was my 50th addition, and I might take it out for future use. The likely quick loss of it into the enemy's hands is a big negative in my opinion, and doesn't work as well in a deck full of several smaller to midrange minions.


Cut Cards ✂️

Devil's Egg

Getting these early and burrowing them has won me a few games back in the 40/20 days, but it's not consistent enough to get that off. So otherwise, they often just don't work fast enough to be worth it, or are completely dead draws in the late game. Add that they can potentially come back to haunt you in teh right situation, and it's just not worth the hassle.


Maddening Bells

Have come back to haunt me much more often than they've helped. Especially with AoA's movement ability, you don't want to constrain yourself to one part of the board like that.


Headless Haunt

Yes, 3 cost 4 power is amazing, but the randomness was useless to me in games maybe 50% of the time. When it works, it's great, but when it doesn't it just loses you games.


Palliburrie Bats / Highland Falconer

See my note under Tooth Faeries. I never feel like I'm building value when I cast these guys.


Credits 🎉

Shawn for getting me into this game, and spending way too much time theorycrafting and playing test games.

Pascal for being a great hang at Gen Con and also helping with playtesting!

CJ for being a great guy in general and helping me with a few suggestions (Bower of Bliss helped win me a Gen Con game!)

Nvekm for the original Birds list - it made me realize AoA was always going to be my favorite avatar!


Hope to get to see you, dear reader, at any events I may attend in the future!
