deckinfo.name: Avatar of Earth Midrange
deckinfo.primer:
Utilise the power of [[Avatar of Earth]] to crush your foes. [[Avatar of Earth]] is currently the avatar with the highest potential power in the game! You can realistically get your Avatar up to 5 or 6 power when attacking relatively easily, particularly if you utilise [[Atlas Wanderers]] and [[Earthquake]] to rearrange your opponent's sites so they're nestled in amongst your earth sites.


The deck utilises the most efficient minions earth has to offer in [[Autumn Unicorn]], [[Pudge Butcher]] and [[Atlas Wanderers]], as well as some utility minions in [[Kettletop Leprechaun]], and some other efficient beaters / Root Spider removal / Roots of Yggdrasil insurance in [[Bluecap Knockersl]].


[[Holy Ground]] helps keep the aggro decks at bay. Your [[Common Sense]] toolkit includes mobility spells in [[Blink]] and [[Grapple Shot]], direct damage from [[Magic Missiles]] and [[Duel]], artifact and aura removal from [[Dispel]], creature or artifact removal from [[Bury]].


Earth alone can have a hard time closing the game out, which is where [[Rhongomyniad]], [[Rolling Boulder]], [[Duel]], [[Magic Missiles]] and [[Stone Rain]] can help you catch the more evasive avatars trying to run from you.


All in all, you're trying to use efficiency, raw power and some tactical flexibility to get the job done!

deckinfo.name: Unland Cup 2025 3rd place - AoE Earth-Air Midrange
deckinfo.primer:
Played in Unland Cup in Seattle, June 2025

Went 6-0 in Swiss, then lost in semifinals to Archimago in top 8.


I consider this a standard AoE deck. It goes for consistency, midrange minons, and attacking with the avatar asap with a few spells as finishers.

I played okay but not great, but did well mostly because I lucked out that AoE worked well in the meta and many players were unfamiliar with AoE. I played against 2 Archi decks in 5 games 3-2. If they drew Divine Healing I lost, if they didn't I won. Infiltrate on my large minions was a big problem both when it happened and in making me afraid to play them. Doing it again I would use more Hunter's Lodge and/or Watchtowers. Otherwise the deck worked pretty much like I hoped and was very consistent.


How I Play

Main goal is getting opponent to death's door asap, well before they get me there. Usually this happens by playing a few sites and minions then beating on enemy sites. Getting last hit can be a challenge but there are several cards that can do it and I'll do my best to save one of them for that purpose.


Mulligan

The deck needs 3 earth and 1 air threshold. The air usually isn't needed in the early turns but I do try to have exactly 1 threshold in my opening hand. Windmill is preferred but the extra mana from tower is also nice. Try to get at least one Land Surveyor or Kettletop.


Typical / preferred early game

Turn 1 - Earth site, prefer soldier token

Turn 2 - Earth site, Land Surveyor or Kettletop. Alternately Crusade.

Turn 3 - Third site, hopefully Earth because you had a Windmill or drew fourth site from a minion. Autumn Unicorn. I usually save Root Spider for a specific need.

Turn 4 or 5 - When you have the mana, play Atlas Wanderers and swap the middle 2 sites. Earthquake can also be used. Ideally you get one or two sites from minions or a Core and never need to tap to draw a site.

Later - Step forward and pound the enemy site that is now surrounded by your earth sites.


Sometimes it makes sense to Grapple Shot your Avatar across instead especially if they have earth sites.


Weaknesses

Mostly having lots of minions to defend and damage to get me to DD first.

Gnome Hollows is annoying especially when played in the site in front of their avatar.


A great use of Root Spider is to place under your avatar so enemy minions cannot defend the site.

Royal Bodyguard allows you to attack while on DD.


Cards

Vivien and Rhitta are not essential and could be swapped out. Biggest downside to Rhitta is the 6 cost and I don't want to play that many sites. Philo Stone is not a must either.

I used to have 4 Grapple Shots but kept finding myself not needing them as often. 4 might still be better.

There is no Whirling Blades because it needs 2 Air.

Straight up aggro, get in there as quick as you can, don't let up the pressure. [[Blink]], [[Grapple Shot]] and [[Whirling Blades]] to get your [[Battlemage]] in their faces or deliver the death blow. The latter two spells also help accelerate your damage in the midgame as they can be used in addition to attacking on a turn.


You have direct damage finishers in [[Chain Lightning]] (your Battlemage should be able to get nearby!) and [[Lightning Bolt]] if attacking to deal the death blow isn't possible.


The artifacts are designed to deal with different threats / enemy gameplans - [[Flaming Sword]] for chump blockers and villagers, and [[Screaming Skull]] for spread out little minions. [[Rolling Boulder]] helps soften up larger minions or get the killing blow across the board, or kill pesky [[Daperyll Vampire]]s.


[[Torshammar Trinket]] can also help your [[Battlemage]] take on larger enemies, and it's even got some inbuilt resistance to being removed from the board, which can be a concern for your other artifacts.


If you want to try more high-end you can put in [[Grandmaster Wizard]], [[Highland Clansmen]] and/or [[Ultimate Horror]], but you might find you don't want them because you can't play sites and attack with your [[Battlemage]] on the same turn!

deckinfo.name: Full Sprint Battlemage (3 Color)
deckinfo.primer:
The goal with this list is to close in on the enemy Avatar fast and hard, you'll find that the shorter your games are the more you'll win. Your win condition is to not only attack with your [[Battlemage]] every turn, but to double-up on his damage with [[Critical Strike]], [[Grapple Shot]], or [[Leap Attack]]. Ideally you should save your strike spells for after you've increased your power with: [[Overpower]], [[Torshammar Trinket]], or best of all [[Flaming Sword]]; doubling the value of those spells. I like to conceptualize this deck as having a turbo, beat-down, aggro playstyle, but it is almost certainly more accurate to call it combo. It can really depend on match-up.


When you mulligan you will want to look for a turn 2 [[Flaming Sword]]. This can be accomplished with the combination of any 2 of the following: turn 1 [[Dwarven Forge]], turn 1 Core, turn 2 [[Imperial Road]], or turn 2 Tower. Obviously you will also want the [[Flaming Sword]] in your opening 3 spells. [[Grapple Shot]] is your ideal turn 3 spell, especially if it can connect with their avatar, and thus should also be considered in the mulligan. If that plan doesn't work then you can lean on [[Common Sense]]. Use it to find whatever piece can most suit you in the moment or maybe set up for a big combo turn. This should go without saying but [[Philosopher's Stone]] is also a very powerful early play. With 3 elements in the deck it can cheat a lot of mana for you, for example; [[Common Sense]] into [[Grapple Shot]] + [[Critical Strike]] costs 4 instead of 7! You may want to draw from the atlas on turn 1 to secure threshold for the game, but after that you should only draw from the spellbook. [[Observatory]] is made better in this deck by [[Common Sense]] as it allows you to shuffle away cards you don't want. Only spend about 3 turns playing sites if possible, you want to put your opponent on a clock. Be sure you get 4 mana though. The dream opening hand probably looks something like: [[Philosopher's Stone]], [[Flaming Sword]], [[Common Sense]], [[The Colour Out of Space]], [[Imperial Road]], and any Tower.


By default your time to kill is 8 attacks/strikes. When playing your hand you will want to determine how to lower this number by as much as possible. Note that simply by increasing your power by 1 for each stike (such as with [[Torshammar Trinket]] or [[Flaming Sword]]), you lower that count by 2! Once you are in enemy territory you want to stick close to their avatar to put pressure on, attacking their site to avoid taking a strike back (unless of course you've cast [[Critical Strike]]). Something you will want to be aware of if your opponent starts to stack blockers on their avatar is how [[Flaming Sword]] + [[Leap Attack]] interact. When you resolve [[Leap Attack]] while wielding [[Flaming Sword]], you will deal your power (likely 4) * the number of enemies there to each of those said enemies. Even if they only have a single minion there, that is still 8 damage to both the avatar and the minion! This is an incredibly powerful punish and should always be front of mind.


When it comes time to deliver the death blow you may be quiet hurt, perhaps you even end up at death's door yourself. If so, you can simply use [[Truesight Crossbow]], [[Lightning Bolt]], or [[Minor Explosion]] to finish them off safely, though be aware of that double fire threshold. By staying on top of the enemy avatar, [[Truesight Crossbow]] can also help invalidate blockers given that ranged strikes cannot be defended. [[Lightning Bolt]] is great at catching particularly mobile avatars while [[Minor Explosion]] is better if opponents stack units. These 3 aforementioned cards also help deal with a site that would otherwise be an absolute hoser to this deck, [[Gnome Hollows]]. If your opponent nestles their avatar in there, you will need to dig for these spells as without them you will be unable to deliver the death blow at all. Alternatively you can shut them down with [[Smokestacks of Gnaak]]. Luckily, [[Minor Explosion]] and [[Lightning Bolt]] can each be searched out with [[Common Sense]] so it shouldn't be too hard to find the death blow. You should also be highly concerned about healing, especially [[Daperyll Vampire]], she is a kill on sight threat. [[Poisonous Dagger]] or any power increasing card + any one-sided strike are your best answers pre-sideboarding. If you can't kill her then try to make as much distance as possible and/or get your opponent to death's door ASAP. A final thing to watch out for (though there isn't much to be done about it in main deck) is [[Atlantean Fate]]. With only 3 ordinary sites in the atlas, this aura can be completely debilitating. When it comes out you will simply be forced to slow down and take more space to recover threshold.


The sideboard is still very much a work in progress, almost all my games have been best of 1. You may have noticed that I include [[Font of Life]] despite not having many water sites in the deck. This tech is specifically for playing into water decks that play [[Flood]] and [[Atlantean Fate]], capitalizing on the threshold these cards provide you. There is also a [[Disenchant]] which can take care of [[Atlantean Fate]] if needed. It can also be helpful in mirror matches with other [[Battlemage]]s, be careful not to fire it off when you're standing with them! You could instead use [[Telekinesis]] to take whatever gear they are stacking, or more generally take away alchemy 9 pieces from opponents. Depending on what elements your opponent is playing, [[Bury]] or [[Drown]], along with [[Infiltrate]], are for dealing with decks that can go late despite your best efforts to rush them down (looking at you [[Pathfinder]]). Save them for big threats or those pesky [[Daperyll Vampire]]s. [[Divine Healing]] is also for games you expect to go longer and thusbcan spend the time setting up threshold. Finally there is [[Poison Nova]] which can serve to answer any unit(s), be they big or many. As for what to take out for any of these tools... I have no clue! Like I said before, my games have been nearly all Bo1. Probably remove the extra copies of ordinaries (excluding [[Common Sense]] and [[Grapple Shot]]), cut [[Screaming Skull]] if they don't play many early minions... I really don't know for sure.


My final note is that while I think this deck is in a decently refined state, it is a copy of the deck I play in paper and some choices have been influenced by personal card pool constraints. Hope you like it if you try it and I welcome comments!

deckinfo.name: Mobility BM - 2nd place Lobstercon & Toy Drive
deckinfo.primer:
History

This deck was based on the Blazing Battlemage deck from Beta. It's been updated to incorporate more Fire mobility in AL as well as focus on dealing damage quickly.


Philosophy

BM is obviously your main source of damage dealing along with 11 direct damage spells. Consider charge minions as more direct damage as if you'll always hit once and if they use removal, you're okay with that. If they stick around for a second swing, you're ahead! Pair this with a slew of ramping artifacts and utility relics, games go super quick with this deck (either you'll win fast or you'll lose fast).


Battlemage

Like all BM decks, BM needs to use life as a resource. There's nothing better than killing a minion and drawing that sweet extra card. If you can screaming skull or crown, you'll end up ahead very quickly. Don't be afraid to clear early minions by directly attacking them as this is essentially card advantage.



Cards

Mobility

4 key cards for movement: Blink, Grapple Shot, Blaze, and our new favorite from AL: War Horse. All these cards are self-explanatory but getting to 4 mana and traversing across the board at the same time is the goal with BM. You never need more than 5 sites and rarely a 6th (assuming you want to play two spells a turn).


Minions

As explained above, all the charge minions are used as direct damage. Rarely do you want to use them as removal (or trading with their minions). Ideally you let BM eat their minions so you can get another card and more damage in. Pressure on their life is critical. People play differently when they're at 12 versus 18.


Morgana is a new add to this deck and she's just too good not to use. Boudicca is a monster and can help you win from behind with 2 attacks. Finally, Courtesan is a easy choice as a finisher, especially if you get trapped or far away in a door/door situation.


Artifacts

Cores and Stone are good to ramp. Don't rely on them all game though. Just a Rock, Disenchants, Cave-ins are very popular right now so it's best to use the Cores to get ahead, but still get 4-5 sites down ASAP. Ring is King.... if you get Ring going with Trinkets, it's almost guaranteed victory. I've heard to hold Ring back until you start to need the life gain. Often you can bait their disenchant using a core/stone/ring... then you can drop your Skull, Crown, or Rhong, and watch them be salty.


Magic

Beyond direct damage and movement spells, removal and utility spells are far and few but still needed in the clutch. Disenchant, Disintegrate, Shatter Strike, and Poison Nova can and will be used throughout your gameplay. Warp Spasm is a new add... we'll see if it plays dividends


Sites

Standard mix of Fire/Air. You'll see that I heavily reduced air for the 2025 build due to double air being very tough at times. Mirage is amazing with Fields if you need to bounce. Save Funeral Pyres for Archimago decks to get rid of their fuel. Forge has been a good add to allow for the first strike and saving health on BM. Finally, Poisoned Well almost always get 2 damage and boy does that free dmg add up. Ensure you position your River of Flame not in the middle column so you have options to finish with line of sight.


Beware

Bad Matchups

Aggro can be hard. You'll need to stomach through their onslaught, but I think this deck will consistently beat Fury Road now

Control is easy. You do too much damage too quickly and opponents will be sad. New players will think BM is the most imba Avatar if they play a medium/slow deck

Mirror is 55/45 in our favor. This BM has more utility than the normal build. I'm confident it beats the mirror


Cards that BLOW us out

Gnome Hollows is bane of our existence. We can play around it though!! Focus on getting other site damage and finish with Bolt or Bolts. Save Smokestacks if you think you'll be against GH.

Valor is something you need to learn to play around. If I'm on opposing avatar square and they're playing earth and have another minion... the right play is to directly attack the minion. Valor can only defend the site or another ally. So they'll have to use their avatar and thus take the damage anyways.



2025 changes - mostly shifting away from Double Air

-3 Gyre Hippogryff, +1 Morgana la Fey, +2 Saracen Raiders

-1 Arc Lightning, +1 Warp Spasm

-1 Highland Princess, +1 Rhongomyniad

-1 Lone, -1 Dark, -1 Gothic, +2 Funeral Pyre, +1 Poisoned Well


There were times that double air cards were in my hand all game and trying to draw through your atlas for that second air was hard. There were also times where I wanted to stop at 4 sites, but I only had double red so I couldn't cast Boudicca. So with the inclusion of Morgana, dropping all double air cards seemed to be the best choice. Saracen Raiders are arguably better than Hippos and while Princess was great for grabbing Ring, she's not worth that threshold. Morgana more than makes up for 1 less creature.


Other considerations... I did like Arc Lightning as a finisher because it's not random and it can also take down a Vamps, but with inclusion of Shatter Strike, I think we'll be good. In fact, I might go 2 Shatter Strike if Warp Spasm doesn't work out. I'm mostly trying to use Rhong for the first strike and throw it for a finisher or to get on DD... but I don't have many reps with it yet so we'll see how it goes. It's expensive so it might prove to be too slow.


Thanks for reading and contact me on Discord (Phobeef) if you have any questions!

deckinfo.name: Gen Con 2023 Tournament Winner - Jarrett Messing's Impstorm  (Deathspeaker Air/Fire)
deckinfo.primer:
I find myself in the surprising position to provide insight into the deck that won the Sorcery constructed tournament at Gen Con 2023. You might find this less of a deck tech and more of my thought process going into the event. The decisions that led me to this deck were as much personal as game related. The former, the personal, is inherently so specific as to be rarely addressed in analysis, but it is an equally important element in tournament success. I don't have any astonishing insights into how to build a meta-breaking, tournament-dominating deck. This is more of a lesson in how to stumble forward with what you know.


I prepared with a pair of assumptions:


1) It seemed likely that Air/Earth midrange would be the predominant build. Early successes established this as the preeminent powerhouse, and with limited card supply I suspected this would be one of the easier decks to build for folks who didn't pledge or pledge big. Much of the power is in the ordinary and exceptional slots, and many of the key cards are contained in the preconstructed decks, including one of the best avatars for it (Earth). A Pathfinder based version of this deck seemed on the verge of winning the second season of the TTS league. It's just a damn good, consistent deck that runs a lot of the best cards in the game, capable of big bursts of damage, strong board presence, board manipulation, burst healing, with great removal and maneuver.  


2) I would be playing [[Deathspeaker]]. It seemed close in power to the air/earth deck, if a bit less consistently good, and I had far more reps with it in and out of the TTS league. I did not have time to deviate from my comfort zone and get sufficient practice with anything before the con. The goals of the deck are straightforward. Draw as much as possible through recursion, don't allow heavy hitters to stick around, and maximize damage until you can [[Major Explosion]] or [[Nimbus Jinn]] the opponent to Death's Door. Finishers abound. Pretty simple, right? 


My most difficult choice came down to elements: Air/Earth/Fire, Air/Earth or Air/Fire? Air has the wizards for the card draw, so that was automatic, and Alpha Thunderstorm*. Earth has possibly the best overall suite of spells. Fire offers some of the best options for Deathspeaker in [[Vile Imp]] and [[Death Dealer]], one of the best removal spells in [[Infiltrate]], and best damage in Major Explosion. Take all three perhaps? Well, truthfully, there are more good options with the three elements than fit in a deck, and taking all three elements comes with the cost. Occasionally you will bump into a threshold problem and that can throw a wrench in things, especially if you're running triple threshold cards like [[Divine Healing]] and [[Browse]]. This makes you more dependent on Cores which can be ripped away at inconvenient times. There were three main reasons I decided against Earth. The [[Avatar of Earth]], playing into Earth, is especially devastating. She can grapple across the table with impunity as you're bolstering her with your own sites. I want my opponent to stay on their side of the table. Also, I knew of several off-meta Water decks in attendance, and suspected more. Water hampers many of Earth's best spells. Thirdly, Earth seemed like the slower road to the end game. [[Wraetannis Titan]] requires Sphere offensively, [[Craterize]] is a turn and a tax behind Major Explosion, and healing is prolongation, not acceleration. I felt like I would want the most linear path to Death's Door possible, and to win a race in the mirror match. 


Somewhat ironically, my game 5 finals opponent, Adam (Zalem), consistently one of the best Sorcery players throughout the league and playtests, helped solidify my choice and finalize my deck. After hammering out my idea on Curiosa I decided to see if anyone was running something similar. Lo, Zalem had built an Air/Fire Deathspeaker deck! And it was nearly identical! This gave me a huge confidence boost. His differences were one less Thunderstorm and an additional two [[Chaos Twister]]. I liked my four [[Firebolts]], and I hadn't considered the latter at all in any kind of serious format. But upon checking the Twister FAQ, and with some consideration I saw the incredible upside. You are very likely to remove the target, between the void and sites, and with some luck you have a potential 2-for-1 by slinging it into another minion, or direct damage by hitting the opposing avatar. Funnily enough, when I told this to Zalem, he said it was one of his cuts before the event due to inconsistency! 


Key Cards

[[Thunderstorm]]. *A note on Alpha Thunderstorm. This event used the RAW version of Thunderstorm, the Alpha high T version. It's extremely powerful as it ticks down only when you shoot a bolt, and can linger and move until exhausted. 4 mana, 9 damage. This is amazing, almost immediate pressure. Thunderstorm pairs extremely well with some of the other spells and sites in the deck. Fire's Deserts can clear bolt-absorbers, as can Firebolts, assuring the bolts hit the enemy avatar. I wasn't going to play this event without three. This card will be brought in line for Beta. Three Thunderstorms was a winning choice.


[[Infiltrate]]

Arguably the best removal spell in the game, this card takes your opponent's minion from them and gives you control of that minion with stealth until they deal damage. Notably, when attacking an undefended enemy site, you cause a loss of life rather than damage. Incredible potential, and a huge swing when you can eliminate a beater. I was particularly keen on this as if I stole a 5-power minion from an Earth deck I would now be able to trade their minion with another of their 5-power beaters. 


[[Summoning Sphere]]

Part of the win condition of this deck, a Summoning Sphere + Imp can finish an avatar on Death's Door. It allows me to play a Djinn and dump my hand to bring an avatar to 0. Alternatively, a sphere opener can allow me to play an Imp on their avatar turn 2, which puts a lot of pressure on the opponent to spend removal or get their own minion out at home. 


[[Vile Imp]]

The magnificent Imp! Pinpoint damage, harassment, finishing blow all in an inexpensive and annoying body. 


Apprentice/[[Grandmaster Wizard]]

Draw/Draw more. X2. Maybe x3 or x4 with Geistwood and Pact.


[[Major Explosion]]

The finisher. It's very hard to do sufficient chip damage to finish off an avatar, even with Thunderstorm. Seven mana is not that difficult to cast, and you're often one move away from launching this across the table. The 5 damage splash zone clears Earth heavies. It has the added benefit of clearing the immediate area of Thunderstorm bodyguards. 


[[Highland Falconer]]/[[Sacred Scarabs]]

Exploding flying bugs! Easy four damage and 2-for-1 retrieval. I got rid of scarabs with mulligans every game I drew them in my opening hand. Better to draw some kind of ramp or a recurrable falconer to fetch one. 


So it all worked out! It took some luck as it always does, but the deck performed extremely and consistently well. I stayed within myself, and the flow of play was very familiar despite the lack of reps with this particular build. Most importantly, I played five great opponents who were a pleasure to share the table with, foremost among them being Adam in the final. Nerves came with the stakes, but the game could not have been more friendly. And, despite his rough opening, he had me on Death's Door and was one turn away from snatching away the victory! Wild end to the event!

deckinfo.name: Deathspeaker Jinn Combo
deckinfo.primer:
The [[Deathspeaker]] can come from anywhere and win the game. You can be down at Death's Door, dodge your way out and drop some big bombs on your opponent and still take out the win.


The plan here is to use your early disruption and ramp to stall the game until turn 6 or 7, when you can hopefully consistently double or triple spell, and finish with big hitters like [[Major Explosion]] and [[Nimbus Jinn]] combo.


[[Highland Princess]] lets you get way ahead with a [[Philosopher's Stone]] leading to crazy discounts (sometimes 3 mana a turn!)


[[Minor Explosion]], [[Vile Imp]], [[Sacred Scarabs]], [[Firebolts]] and your other removal can help keep you alive. [[Summoning Sphere]] can also let you finish the game with a reanimated [[Vile Imp]] when your opponent is at Death's Door.


Make sure you keep the board absolutely clear, dodge those big [[Grapple Shot]]s and don't get too far behind too early.


The deck also has [[The Geistwood]], [[Grandmaster Wizard]] and [[Apprentice Wizard]] package for card advantage, which can let you get seriously ahead on cards. Use that when you need, but also don't be afraid to prioritise interaction when you can.

deckinfo.name: Candlemas Snacks - DS Combo
deckinfo.primer:
Arthurian Legends Primer update coming soon! Shoutout to @MV for finding the Britomart interaction for guaranteed infinite turns!


Greetings, Sorcerers! Or...Deathspeakers, rather!


Welcome to the mysterious realm of combo in Sorcery. Given the current small card pool in the game, there aren't very many true combo decks yet but this one comes pretty close. This deck can still play a good midrange value game with the classic [[Deathspeaker]] package of minions with Genesis abilities but offers different end-game options for players who want to spice things up a bit.

Typically, [[Deathspeaker]] control/combo tends to use [[Summoning Sphere]] and [[Nimbus Jinn]] or just [[Ruler of Thul]] and a swarm of small minions to put the opponent to Death's Door in one or two turns very late into the game. While [[Nimbus Jinn]] or a swarm of small minions can certainly still be a reasonable path to victory for this deck, the real closers are combining [[Crave Golem]] with [[Candlemas Monks]] or winning with [[The Immortal Throne]].

For anyone who isn't familiar with the Golem/Monks combo, the goal is pretty straight forward but, pulling it off in a way that gets you multiple extra turns in a row can be tricky. If you have [[Kythera Mechanism]], the Golem is much easier to control but without that, you will need to place and move your minions in a very careful manner so that the Golem is always eating the right diet.

[[The Immortal Throne]] can also be a difficult card to use effectively as you rarely want to give your opponent extra cards. With [[Deathspaker]]'s ability having access to both Cemeteries, you'll typically be able to cast a spell with the right mana cost to trigger the Throne.


The Gameplan


So, how does this deck actually play out? First, let's cover some of the basics of operation before getting into the finer details and individual card choices.


Like most [[Deathspeaker]] decks, this list includes a fairly standard package of [[Vile Imp]]s, [[Land Surveyor]]s, and Wizards. This minion suite allows you to keep the card advantage flowing while you chump block your way into the late game. From there your combo pieces can - and typically will - come together to achieve victory. In the early stages of the game, [[Land Surveyor]], [[Vile Imp]], [[Highland Princess]], and [[Apprentice Wizard]] are all fantastic cards to have. These small minions will help develop your hand and board while absorbing incoming damage from the opponent's attacks. Sacrificing your minions to block larger enemies will often result in your opponent over-committing minions to the board which sets you up for good Earthquake and Poison Nova turns. As you play, really try to look for opportunities to set up 2-for-1 or better trades with your removal even if that means taking a bunch of damage or losing a few minions in one turn to set up the sweep on the following turn. As you play the early game, you can get in some small chip damage with your 2 or 3-drop minions but it is rare that these small attacks will end up mattering much in the end; make the attacks if they're free but it's ok to be overcautious and just leave stuff back to block surprise attacks.


Once you've arrived at the the end-game, where do you go from this point? (The end-game being the point by which you have enough combo pieces to start drawing a ton of extra cards and/or taking multiple turns in a row with Golems+Monks, or both...or, your opponent has dealt so much damage to you before you can stabilize, that you are forced to try to combo even if it's not guaranteed to work out. Understanding at what point you have entered the late-game - and at what point to start actually going for the combo - is very tricky to decipher in every match-up and it just takes a lot of practice to get familiar with. One question that this deck keeps asking me is this:

"You have [[Crave Golem]] and [[Candlemas Monks]] at your disposal. Do you play them both out and take a single extra turn with no guarantee that you will be able to continue taking extra turns? Or, do you continue to hold onto the combo pieces until you are sure that you can take 3-5 turns in a row and usually ensure that you will win?"

In most cases, I've found that while taking the single extra turn as soon as possible feels good in the short-term, it is usually better to wait until you know you can take multiple extra turns in a row rather than just one. Occasionally however, it is correct to take just a single extra turn right away if you can. Understanding when that is the case is incredibly difficult and is still something that I don't feel I've mastered even after 50+ matches with the deck.


Another question this deck asks is:

"When you decide to start going for the multiple extra turns, do you want to be at Death's Door or not?"

If you are going to take 3-6 turns in a row but really need to draw extra cards off of [[The Immortal Throne]] or dead [[Grandmaster Wizards]] to close the game out, it can be much easier to do that if you are at Death's Door and casting from Cemeteries is free. If you don't know that the extra turns available to you will be enough to win the game before your opponent gets a turn, then it's usually not a good idea to go to Death's Door by choice. It is often the case that being at Death's Door when you start to combo guarantees your win whereas being at 1 or more life (not being able to cast dead minions for free) is more of a gamble. Luckily, if you know that being at Death's Door will guarantee your victory, your opponents are likely to want you at Death's Door and will help you out with that by attacking. If your opponent is being less cooperative, you can often put yourself to Death's Door with [[Vile Imp]] or [[Lightning Bolt]] while still having the mana and resources needed to start the combo. If you are trying to win with [[The Immortal Throne]], you usually need fewer extra turns than you would if you were trying to win by attacking with your minions over the course of extra turns. 2 or 3 extra turns in a row is often enough to win with the Throne but if you are trying to win through attacking, you'll need 3-5 turns in most situations. One thing to keep in mind is that even though you are essentially skipping your opponent's turn with the combo, they do still get to untap and they do still get an end phase. If they have something like [[Angel's Egg]], [[Devil's Egg]], or [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]], they will get to trigger those things in their "skipped" turn's End Phase.


Individual Card Explanations


[[Kythera Mechanism]] - This is a very important card when you are trying to take multiple turns in a row. Mechanism allows you to better control where [[Crave Golem]] goes and what it eats. It also allows [[Raise Dead]] to continue bringing back [[Candlemas Monks]] even if there are other minions in Cemeteries. Look out for other decks with [[Kythera Mechanism]] because whoever controls the most recent Mechanism controls random outcomes. If you see your opponent has [[Headless Haunt]] or [[Thunderstorm]] it can be tempting to play your Mechanism out to control them but if your opponent plays their own Mechanism later, your's will be shut off and it will be more difficult to sustain your combo. If you find yourself needing to combo without it, you usually have to get pretty creative.


[[Mix Aer]]/[[Mix Ignis]] - The Mixes allow you to go for combo turns sooner or, cast an early [[Major Explosion]] or [[Grandmaster Wizard]] if needed. The 1 mana cost makes them fetchable with [[Highland Princess]] and trigger [[The Immortal Throne]]. [[Mix Ignis]] and [[Scavenging Fiend]] is a cute little combo. Just remember to summon the Fiend on a site with a Spellcaster so that the Mix isn't sitting somewhere it can't be used.


[[Angel's Egg]] - Surviving early damage output is the most important goal for this deck and gaining a little life each turn goes a long way. Remember to gain your life on the end step of the "skipped" turns!


[[Crave Golem]] - While this card is a key combo piece for the deck it still has great utility in various non-combo situations. It can often trade for two of your opponent's smaller minions which is fantastic against aggro. It can also be very useful for eating your own minions with Genesis abilities so that you can keep a well-stocked Cemetery for your Deathspeaker. It's a real sweet thing to have a [[Grandmaster Wizard]] on a [[Geistwood]] get eaten by the Golem. You'll just be drowning in card advantage. Make sure you familiarize yourself with the FAQ entries for [[Crave Golem]] as there are a lot of really weird interactions and restrictions with the card. For example, the Golem has to follow normal attacking rules when using it's triggered ability except that it can attack friendly minions. So, if the Golem attacks one of your minions, you can have other minions you control block the attack. This typically comes up in cases where you've played a [[Candlemas Monks]] slightly out of the Golem's reach but still in a position where they can move to block for a friendly minion being attacked by the Golem.


[[The Immortal Throne]] - This card is insanely powerful and you can often win in just two turns with it depending on the situation. The turn you play the Throne, you'll usually want to immediately be able to draw 2-3 cards off of it. Getting the Throne up to 3 counters is the best way to allow your opponent to draw a card or two on their next turn. While the opponent drawing cards is never a great feeling, you have a better shot of winning with the Throne the following turn if your opponent has helped you tick it up. With Mixes and a free summon from the Cemetery, it can be very easy for you to cast a 5-mana, a 6-mana, and a 7-mana spell all in the same turn and with with the Throne.


[[Undertaker Engine]] - If you want to win with [[The Immortal Throne]], you've got to have some 7-mana spells. While 7 mana for a 4 power minion isn't exciting, the ability to burrow/unburrow things can be very useful. The Throne will still trigger to draw cards if it has been buried but you can't win the game if it is underground with 8 counters. [[Undertaker Engine]] allows you to tick the Throne up to 8 counters and unburrow it at the end of the turn so that you win.


[[Candlemas Monks]] - The other half of the combo and definitely a weaker card compared to [[Crave Golem]]. Monks is rarely used outside of the combo but they can block in a pinch, attack if you're ahead, and offer some protection against [[Roots of Yggdrasil]] decks. Preventing the opponent from having a follow-up spell after popping Roots is nice.


[[Scavenging Fiend]] - This card is awesome! It was one of my favorite cards when I started playing the game and I'm really happy that it has a home here. This deck has a lot of useful artifacts and being able to get 2 artifacts back per Fiend thanks to [[Deathspeaker]] feels really amazing.


[[Nimbus Jinn]] - I don't think that there is room in this deck for [[Summoning Sphere]] but I still think that Jinn is a fantastic card here. The deck also needs 6-mana spells for the Throne and options are limited.


[[Browse]] - Triple Air threshold can be tough to get at times but [[Browse]] is the best way to piece together a stable combo.


[[Disenchant]] - [[Battlemage]] is a tough matchup and [[Screaming Skull]] is your worst nightmare so having access to a copy of [[Disenchant]] feels extremely important for this deck. You don't have [[Common Sense]] to be able to find it easily but you will usually draw enough cards over the course of the game to have a good shot at finding it.


[[Raise Dead]] - This card is typically necessary for chaining together multiple extra turns and if you don't have [[Kythera Mechanism]] you're going to need to clear out the chaff from the Cemeteries in order to make this a useful spell. Any time that you have extra mana lying around, consider casting a minion from a Cemetery just to get it out of the way of future [[Raise Dead]]s.


[[Earthquake]], [[Poison Nova]], [[Major Explosion]], and [[Death Dealer]] - access to 5 sweeper cards feels like a good spot to be. With how many cards you see in an average game, you'll rarely be unable to find at least one of these and one is often enough to get things stabilized.


[[Boneyard]] - The fact that your opponent gets to summon a minion as well means that you will often need a bit of setup before you're able to use [[Boneyard]] but when it's good, it's amazing.


[[Gnome Hollows]] - This site is excellent at slowing the game down so that you have time to set up. It can also be used to protect your own minions from [[Grave Golem]] or to at least affect a Golem's path. Be aware that if you you have [[The Immortal Throne]] on a [[Gnome Hollows]] and it gets buried, you'll almost never be able to bring it back up with [[Undertaker Engine]].


Wrapping Up


Overall, this deck has a lot of consistency and recursion for combo pieces so as long as you're patient, you should be able combo in most of your games. This deck has required a ton of practice but it is super fun once you start to get the hang of it. This is also a gross combo deck that may make your opponents hate you, or hate the game, so you should definitely feel guilty for playing it ;)


If you have any questions or comments, don't hesitate to post them!

deckinfo.name: JOHNNY FIRELORD (2nd Place Explorer Series KY)
1st Place GenCon HOT SPRINGS
deckinfo.primer:
Hi Team,


Excited to share about the deck, but first would be remiss if I didn't give credit and thanks to my team, Chris @Ismarkthelesser and Nick @Astronomonov, as well as John @PorkchopSandwitches and Blake @Collision for the insight and countless games that provided the context into many of these choices. As much your win as mine!


Also, to Pascal, my finals opponent. Thank you for one of the hardest, funnest, and friendliest games I've ever played. Despite the stakes, I appreciate how we approached the game as though we had already felt like winners just being in the seat, and counter each other. You are a champion.


Hot Spring has been a work in progress for ~8 months, after countless iterations, this is where we have landed currently.


Original deck list of where it all started.


GenCon 2025 Finals Match


Deck spotlight with Chase and EC team.


Now, into the deck.


Weaknesses: Fire and Water offer NO aura hate (outside of Scorched Earth), which means impactful auras stick around. Generally, you can outpace a deck with aura strategies, but not always. This also means no Monument hate either. This wouldn't have been a problem pre-Archimago's rise to fame, but now we're seeing more and more Orbs. Luckily, you are able to capitalize on the orb as well, with double Shatter Strikes and Minor Explosions worst case. This has changed with the inclusion of Swap; however, these problems do persist. Ironically, I think the biggest nemesis to the deck is itself, as in the last 5 major tournaments, I lost in the top 16 or higher against the mirror match. It was my bane.



A quick breakdown of each section of the deck and logic behind the card:


Auras:

  • Jihad: Self-explanatory. One of the most powerful fire cards ever printed. This card allows 5 power Monstrous Lions on turn 3 with a pond.


  • Atlantean Fate: Look at that, also one of the best cards ever printed. This primary function is to allow you to disrupt the Archimago's and other greedy threshold decks. It also provides a path to clear out popular problematic sites, like Free City, Pebbled Paths, and even Perilous Bridges. Also kills root spiders if they are on a sight that can be affected.


Artifact:


  • Torshammar Trinket: Druid can abuse this by always having access to Tawny. Probably a 3 of in most decks at this point.


  • Ring of Morrigan: IMO the strongest card in a vacuum ever printed, but particularly abusable in this deck. In conjunction with Drums, the ability to IG-88 your way through your opponent's team while also gaining life is backbreaking to say the least.


  • Mask of Meyham: With the strike change, we felt this or GG were too valuable to run, but the questions were, which one, and how many copies? Assuming there would be a concentration of Archimagos, we felt 1 Mask and 1 drums was the right call, as drums can feel dead against the few creatures in most Archimago's lists. This has a synergy with Sir Agravaine (we will cover that on his bullet point) and with the concentration of smaller minions, we thought the mask was better than GG.


  • Drums of Doom: Can lock down the game in a (candidly) un-interactive way. In a minion-heavy meta, expect druids to have 2x of these in their deck. Ring + this. Deserts, Tawny, vile Imp, all kill spells now. Also, the only way to protect against Nymbus Djinn otk.


Minions:


  • Polar Explorers: This quickly became one of my favorite cards in the deck. It enables SO much and makes cards like Redcap Poweries and Monstrous Lion have less drawback by evading problematic sites.


  • Vile Imp: 2 damage on entry, Kill spell with Drums. Takes out knights holding lances often and is just one of the best 2 drops in the game.


  • Kobolds: With the 3 of trinkets, and the prominence of Gnome Hollows, these angy little dudes provided, in most cases, bare minimum, 3 extra copies of Vile Imp, but with an insane ceiling. Also combos with strike synergy, kills tough airborne minions like Plumed Pegasus if comboed with deserts or Trinket. Very easy to deal with their tempo play with one of these early.



  • Lugbog Cat: Amazing tempo play with Pond, can reach into opponents' site with Floodplain. Solid beast.


  • Morgana le Fay: Soooo much value with this card. Boneyard target at the very least for more cards. Helps in grindy games.


  • Redcap Powries: Cheapest charge minion for the stats. Almost no downside at this point with the immobilized nerf.


  • ***MVP Sir Agravaine***: Self-protecting unit that buffs Tawny's attacks. Has proven to be a huge problem and is not answered with non-targeting damage. Enables one to turn deaths doors with only a few minions striking the avatar. With the recent attack trigger change, he will always strike the *original* target. Meaning, while adjacent to an enemy avatar being attacked, he will ALWAYS strike the avatar regardless of whether there are blockers around. This singlehandedly won me 2 of my games late in the bracket and is an absolute kill on site card.



  • Boudicca: Buffs Tawny and can just be a sudden death's door machine. Boneyard target for surprise extra damage due to getting value off her passive immediately. (if they aren't already dead by then).


  • Monstrous Lion: Has been one of the biggest standout cards. Combos with Pond, great target for Guyer to be used as a kill spell on a body. Great with all of the Battle Mages, as it gets value immediately, and also serves the 3 power.


  • Selfsame Simulacrum: After the recent revision of how multiple Bruins interact, this became too good not to run, though it never came up in my finals match. With multiple other targets, or your opponent's best minion, plenty of value to be had with this card.


  • Ruler of Thul: Similar role to Boudicca. Burst potential. Awesome surprise play with flipping Druid into Bruin, then following that up on the next turn with a Ruler for 8 in their back row with the free unit in Bruin. Also recursive with Lady of the Lake.


  • Sir Gaheris: Decent stats, and it does play well against many aggro decks, by being able to keep life parity and block, which is nice.


  • Panorama Manticore: Similar role to Phoenix, early bruiser that is hard to deal with. Untaps regularly and trades well.


  • Questing Beast: Also a Bruiser, awesome burst potential with attack from stealth and shatter strike. Mastering the art of the end-of-turn step turns this card from a great card to an absolute menace! With the ability to attack, then step back onto a watersite protects this to get you multiple strikes of 25% of their starting health.



Magics:


  • Geyser: Started out as a way to deal with Root Spider has quickly become one of my favorite cards. Providing airborne to these units increases their lethality dramatically, allowing them to avoid many problematic defensive sites. Also is a good combo with Blaze as it really extends the range with + movement and the ability to fly nearby.


  • Pollimorph: hard removal is pivotal right now with the abundance of 5+ power minions and vampires' abilities to Deaths Door you and heal for a billion while attacking sites. Also, the fact that it banishes the transformed card is actually a huge boon.


  • Minor Explosion: I started with 3 firebolts; however, the prevalence of Morgana Le Fey ultimately had me consider this instead. The indiscriminate 3 damage has a higher ceiling and, with the reach of Tawny, can easily be a 2 for 1.


  • Disintegrate: Similar to Pollimorph. Hard removal easily cast from Tawny.


  • Pact with the Devil: This has been one of my favorite cards. Combining with Tawny, Adept Illusionist, and Morgana (more niche) allows you to keep up with Sorcerer and Archimage in the mid-late game.


  • Swap (Placeholder in deck as Font of Life because they have the same mana and threshold): My friends and I had a feeling this card would be absolutely broken, and it sure felt good. This replaces Shatter Strike in the deck, and I have 0 regrets. Super flexible, and stealing Pstone and Rings while putting your guy directly on them feels AMAZING.


Key Sites:


  • Floodplain: Always been one of my favorites due to its ability to allow you to play more greedy with your threshold in Water, but also serves the purpose to kill root spiders and other burrowed minions and to extend reach on Lugbog cat.


  • Pond: MVP site: So many beasts in the deck make a dramatically increased impact by coming out a turn earlier. Tower for beasts, but better. Also amazing that with the prominence of earth still, being summoned onto a water site protects the beast you curved out from burry effects.


  • Desert: Are key to taking momentum. Also protects against enemies, Atlanian Fate turning off the critical threshold needed to cast key spells.


  • Boneyard: Though I never saw it at gencon, in my testing this card has been an amazing addition to the atlas. With several of the hard removals banishing, and access to Funeral Pyre, you can construct a sided resurrection. Also, with the concentration of charge units, you are able to bring back a Redcap, for instance, and attack with it, and because the unit they brought back entered the same turn, it will have summoning sickness. It also lets you bring back your "Win button" unique for its powerful genesis or passive abilities. Lastly, in what I presumed to be a Archimago heavy meta, the lack of minions they generally have allow this to be onesided even more regularly. It was my favorite spice in the deck.


  • Kelp Cavern: I originally hated this card when it was first printed. I thought the lack of "may" made it unplayable. I was wrong. This lets you comfortably mulligan to get better gas early, then go back and find your spells later when needed. I have been very, very impressed with it.


You may notice a lake of Smokestacks. I found, with a number of key genesis, and the draw cadence of the deck, you end up having to play it earlier than you'd like. This turns off your important sites, like deserts and flood plains, which can be really detrimental. Also, with flooding being an ability, smokestacks removes your ability to flood and kill rootspider. So I found it more detrimental than helpful in many matchups.

deckinfo.name: Sylvan Crusade - 1st S6 - Top 8 ToC 2024
deckinfo.primer:
Welcome to Sorcery's Druidic Order! You have been charged with the sacred duty of reclaiming the holy woodlands. Read on to arm yourself with the knowledge and tools needed to ensure victory!


Ever since the release of Arthurian Legends, I've been quite intrigued by [[Druid]]. In my opinion, this avatar has some of the deepest deck-building options and as such, you never know what you're up against when you see a Druid across the table. The flexibility of build options and three powerful abilities allows Druid to adapt to any metagame. This may or may not actually be a good thing from a game design perspective but it has been a very fun puzzle for me as a deckbuilder.


Sylvan Crusade was designed to attack a very specific expected meta for Season 6 of the TTS League. As this particular list evolves, I'll make notes in the "Card Choices" section to shed light on why certain cards are or are not included based on the current meta. Additionally, I’m going to preserve the original list for posterity.

If you're interested in checking out my other Druid decks, I've included a section at the very end of the primer with links and brief descriptions.


On the surface, Sylvan Crusade looks very similar to the classic Earth/Air Sorcerer Midrange decks of yesteryear and I'm honestly not certain that Druid is a more competitive choice over [[Sorcerer]] for this style of deck. The raw power of Sorcerer is undeniable at this point but, when you start to include a lot of spells that cost 5+ mana, the Sorcerer's ability to cast multiple spells each turn begins to diminish. Is a heavier top end at the expense of card quantity worth it? I think that a lot more testing is required to definitively answer that question but for now, I'm leaning towards yes! Yes, but...you need to leverage the abilities on Druid to make up for the card advantage of Sorcerer.

Historically, the Earth/Air package of beefy minions paired with [[Grapple Shot]] and [[Earthquake]] has been a very effective way to beat Fire-heavy Sorcerer aggro decks like Fury Road or Zalem's Fire/Air deck.

When I was looking at the decks used for qualifier rounds by players in the top cut for Season 6, Sorcerer aggro seemed to have a very hefty meta share. There were also a handful of other aggro decks with [[Flamecaller]], [[Avatar of Air]], and [[Battlemage]]. If players kept with whatever archetypes they used most during the qualifying rounds, there were going to be about 18-19 aggro decks (primarily Sorcerer/Fire), 8-9 [[Archimago]] decks (control or combo), and a small handful of other midrange or combo decks. This data led me to the conclusion that I wanted a deck that had an excellent matchup against Sorcerer aggro while not completely folding to Archimago control. I expected virtually no traditional midrange in this top cut as the general sentiment was that Archimago had pushed it out of the meta.

I considered just going with the old Earth/Air Sorcerer option in the hopes that the card draw would be enough to keep pace with Archimago's overwhelming amount of removal. After some deliberation though, I decided that I wanted to have fun with Druid even if it meant that I was going with a deck that might not be optimal. I still really liked the idea of out-muscling aggro with large Earth minions and I had also seen good results with Grapple Shot paired with [[Bruin]] in my Fire/Air aggro builds. I chose to lean into the aggressive end of the curve a little more to fight Archimago. I figured that most of the control versions were going to have the risk of stumbling on threshold early and the best plan was to try to Door them before they got the threshold to cast [[Divine Healing]]. While the plan of early Death's Door against Archimago is still a good one, some of the cards that I included to pursue this goal ended up being very poor choices.

If I'd had more time to test the deck before top cut submissions were due, I think I would have realized that [[Highland Falconer]] and [[Palliburie Bats]] were not good options for this deck. Despite the fact that they pair well with [[Torshammar Trinket]] and offer some resilience against Earthquake, the reality is that they don't line up well against [[Vile Imp]] and [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]] from the Fire aggro decks and they are particularly bad against all of the [[Magic Missiles]] and [[Firebolts]] from Archimago.

Overall, the deck performed very well though and with a few adjustments, I'm super happy with the current list.


Best cards for specific matchups:


Sorcerer aggro (fire) - [[Bosk Troll]], [[Autumn Unicorn]], [[Daperyll Vampire]], [[Sir Galahad]], [[Earthquake]], [[Whirling Blades]], [[Crusade]], [[Ring of Morrigan]], [[Torshammar Trinket]], [[Shield Maidens]], [[Root Spider]], [[Pillar of Zeiros]], [[Pebbled Paths]], [[Quagmire]], [[Pudge Butcher]]. If your Sorcerer opponent is on Air with Palliburrie Bats, Root Spider becomes much worse and if you're against a Water aggro deck, Earthquake is obviously pretty horrible.


Flamecaller aggro - Same list as above but include [[Funeral Pyre]].


Archimago control - [[Dwarven Digging Team]], [[Shield Maidens]], [[Pudge Butcher]], [[Grandmaster Wizard]], [[Gigantism]], [[Grapple Shot]], [[Whirling Blades]], [[Funeral Pyre]], [[Rift Valley]], [[Kingdom of Agartha]], [[Crusade]], [[Pnakotic Manuscript]].


Avatar of Air - [[Torshammar Trinket]], [[Daperyll Vampire]], [[Sir Galahad]], [[Earthquake]], [[Crusade]], [[Grapple Shot]], [[Whirling Blades]], [[Rift Valley]], [[Ring of Morrigan]]


Mirror Match - [[Torshammar Trinket]], [[Pudge Butcher]], [[Dalcean Phalanx]], [[Root Spider]], [[Earthquake]], [[Grapple Shot]], [[Whirling Blades]].



Card Choices:


[[Bosk Troll]], [[Autumn Unicorn]] - These two minions have some of the most aggressive stat lines in the game and contribute to a critical number of beaters with high power to mana ratios. This is important both for stifling early aggression from aggro opponents and putting solid pressure on Archimago in the early game. Many of the best opening hands include one or both of these cards.


[[Pudge Butcher]], [[Dalcean Phalanx]] - While these minions come with serious mobility restrictions, 5 power for 4 mana is still a fantastic rate and when you pair them with mobility spells such as [[Blink]] or Grapple Shot they become incredibly dangerous. If you don't have mobility options, both of these cards can be a liability against aggro decks. If you are playing against aggro and your opening hand has one or more of these and you don't have Grapple Shot, Blink, or an early minion such as Bosk Troll or Autumn Unicorn, you'll probably want to mulligan them away. Summoning either of these on turn 3 using the extra mana from a Tower is one of the best early plays possible.


[[Root Spider]] - Still one of the best ways to shut down aggro and with Torshammar Trinket, it gets to win the fight against opposing spiders! If you're expecting a Water-heavy meta, or a significant amount of minion-light decks like Archimago or Battlemage, you can certainly trim some number of Root Spiders.


[[Daperyll Vampire]] - While this card has my least favorite art in the whole game, it is an incredibly powerful minion and puts in solid work against most opponents. The list that I used in Season 6 only had one copy of this card and that was a mistake. If you're expecting a lot of aggro in the meta, you should run the full 3 copies. This is one of the best things you can combo with Grapple Shot or [[Whirling Blades]] and it's also dreamy with Torshammar Trinket.


[[Grapple Shot]] - Grapple is still one of the most powerful cards in the game and this list wants the full 4 copies. It is fantastic with any large minion and is particularly sweet with [[Bruin]]. The only downside to Grapple is that you need a minion on the board for it to work and keeping a suitable minion alive can often be a challenge. Being able to flip Druid and immediately Grapple with Bruin is an awesome option.


[[Whirling Blades]] - While this card doesn't work optimally with Dalcean Phalanx and doesn't work at all with Pudge Butcher it is wildly powerful and goes well with just about every other minion in the deck.


[[Earthquake]] - My vote for best Earth card to date! This deck gets to leverage the movement of sites very well with Pudge and Phalanx.


[[Gigantism]] - Another of Earth's most powerful cards here. If you've got 7 mana, Gigantism and Grapple Shot, it's usually enough to Door your opponent in one turn.


[[Blink]] - The best mobility spell there is right now. Blink is necessary for most decks that include things like Pudge Butcher or Dalcean Phalanx and surprise movement is one of the most effective ways to win games.


[[Dwarven Digging Team]] - This card is one of several concessions to the prevalence of Archimago. In many games against Archimago control, your best route to victory is to chip your opponent down to around 15 life and then set up a big attack to Door them on a single turn, thus negating Divine Healing. Being able to build up a small army underground and then pop up for a huge attack is one of the best ways that I've found to accomplish this. Dwarven Digging Team also helps combat enemy Root Spiders. This card is not very good against aggro and I would mulligan it if I was up against Sorcerer, Flamecaller, Avatar of Air, or Battlemage.


[[Kettletop Leprechaun]] - This unassuming little fellow is actually very effective in this deck. Since this deck is interested in going up to 6+ mana - especially if it's a matchup where you want to keep [[Tawny]] around as long as possible - anything that draws a site during the early game is about as good as drawing a spell. Having 2 power makes in considerably better than [[Land Surveyor]] in a deck like this that is looking to get aggressive and even smaller minions can become real threats with Torshammar Trinket and [[Crusade]]. The 4 copies that I had in the original list felt like too many and 2 copies has been feeling pretty good.


[[Shield Maidens]] - Not including this card in my Season 6 list was a mistake. It is incredibly powerful against Fire-heavy aggro and provides your whole team with protection against [[Poison Nova]] from Archimago.


[[Sir Galahad]] - This card looked like it was going to be pretty solid but I was not prepared for just how incredible it actually is in the current meta. It prevents damage from some of the most popular minions such as Vile Imp, Pudge Butcher, Daperyll Vampire, and [[Headless Haunt]]. It is very difficult to kill in combat or with damage-based removal and it even survives [[Chaos Twister]] if it lands on a site (with split power/toughness, Chaos Twister adds both numbers together and divides by 2 before rounding up. This means that Galahad only deals 5 damage if it lands on a site after being targeted by Twister). You can also use Pudge Butcher to fight Galahad if you really need to gain 3 life.


[[Grandmaster Wizard]] - The Season 6 list had a single [[Unlikely Alliance]] as a way to catch back up on cards against Archimago. Alliance worked nicely with Highland Falconer/Palliburie Bats and Tawny/Bruin but with the Falconer/Bats package out of the deck, it just isn't reliable enough. Grandmaster Wizard is 6 mana but it is a guaranteed 3 spells which is exactly what this deck wants on later turns. With 3 copies of Trinket in the deck, the 0-power body isn't completely irrelevant either!


[[Highland Princess]] - Any deck that is running good 1-mana artifacts and can get 2 Air threshold should probably include Princess.


[[Disenchant]] - This is a card that is very meta-dependent and always comes with the risk of being a dead draw. I still think it's probably worth including a single copy but I also think you could easily trim it and be fine.


[[Torshammar Trinket]] - This card is so good with Tawny that I really like including the full 3 copies. It makes most combat situations favorable for you on your turn, can't be hit with removal like Disenchant, and is insane with Ring of Morrigan. I think that Trinket is one of the best cards in the current meta.


[[Ring of Morrigan]] - Ring good.


[[Philosopher's Stone]] - With a good mix of multiple elements, Philosopher's Stone is still among the most useful cards available.


[[Pnakotic Manuscript]] - This card is very good with Tawny but can also be used by Dalcean Phalanx or Pudge Butcher of their movement restrictions are preventing them from being effective. I'm still not 100% certain that this card belongs in this list but I do like it and we'll see how further testing goes.


[[Crusade]] - Once you get to around 20 Earth minions in your deck, Crusade starts looking very appealing. Archimago uses a lot of defensive sites like [[Perilous Bridge]] and [[Gnome Hollows]] and Crusade allows you to skip right over those cards. It's also one of the best ways to fight against [[Jihad]] from the Fire aggro decks. Keep in mind that Bruin is a Earth minion and will get the +1!


[[Feast for Crows]] - while this card is particularly bad against aggro, it is incredibly useful against Archimago. I think that this deck has a good enough matchup against aggro to afford a few cards like this and still be ok.


[[Dark Tower]]/[[Gothic Tower]]/[[Lone Tower]] - The best mana accelerant sites in the game. Jumping the curve on early minions is one of the best paths to victory.


[[Funeral Pyre]] - No Fire, 3 Pyre! Archimago is this much of a problem. Typically decks with threshold requirements like this can afford 3-5 off-element, utility sites. I would love to be able to play more [[Wizard's Den]], [[Sinkhole]], [[Free City]], [[Town]], etc., but stripping Archimago of cards is just too important right now. You'll also be happy to see Pyres against any [[Deathspeaker]] opponents you run across.


[[Glastonbury Tor]]/[[The Colour Out of Space]] - While both of these sites can be a liability against opposing Earthquakes they are a necessary inclusion for the threshold requirements. If you're playing against an Earth opponent, try to spread them out so they can't both be hit by the same Earthquake.


[[Impenetrable Copse]] - Copse is fantastic against Archimago and other decks using Grapple Shot or Pudge Butcher.


[[Kingdom of Agartha]] - There is some tension between this card and the two copies of Earthquake but Kingdom is so good against Archimago that I think it's worth the risk.


[[Mirror Realm]] - It's rare that a deck doesn't want Mirror Realm and this certainly isn't one of those rare decks.


[[Pebbled Paths]]/[[Quagmire]] - These are the two most effective Earth sites when you're facing against Fire aggro. With how much charge is in the meta right now, I think that pretty much all heavy-Earth decks want a good number of these sites.


[[Pillar of Zeiros]] - Deathspeaker has fallen off considerably in past months but the healing effect from Pillar is still very useful.


[[Rift Valley]] - One of the best sites in the game, Rift Valley should be included in just about every Earth deck.


[[Valley of Delight]]/[[Windmill]] - Great fixing for multi-element decks.


[[Watchtower]] - While [[Infiltrate]] isn't seeing as much play right now, it is still out there and one of the best things against your large minions. [[Morgana le Fay]] and [[Phase Assassin]] are also two big metagame players right now.


[[Wizard's Den]] - With very few options for drawing additional spells, Wizard's Den is a welcome inclusion and I wish that I could fit the second copy in here. If you expect less Archimago, you can definitely swap out a Funeral Pyre for an extra Den.


[[Highland Falconer]]/[[Palliburrie Bats]] (currently out of the deck) - This package works really well against decks that use things like [[Bury]] or Earthquake as their primary removal. They are also fantastic at driving out enemy Root Spiders. The two bodies that you get when you cast Falconer are nice with Torshammar Trinket. This package is currently out of the deck because Archimago has a ton of things like Magic Missiles and the Fire aggro decks have Vile Imp and Quarrelsome Kobolds.


[[Unlikely Alliance]] (currently out of the deck) - With the removal of Highland Falconer and Palliburrie Bats, this card just isn't reliable enough.


[[Vanguard Knights]] (currently out of the deck) - I really like that Vanguard Knights can be played off of a turn 1 Earth site into turn 2 Tower (something that Autumn Unicorn can't). It is also really cool that you can sneak the Knights onto Gnome Hollows. If you start their movement as 2-power they don't become 4-power until they're actually on the Hollows. This card can be incredibly awkward and ultimately, I've decided to bench it for now.


[[Atlas Wanderers]] (currently out of the deck) - While the ability on this card can be very useful, the triple Earth threshold and the fact that it isn't significantly more powerful than most of the other minions at the 4-5 mana range led me to cut the single copy that I had in my initial list.


[[Bury]] (currently out of the deck) - The Fire-based aggro decks have tons of small minions that make Bury feel underwhelming. Archimago has virtually no minions that you care about so Bury is just a weaker Disenchant for their artifacts. If non-water midrange makes more of a comeback, I would put Bury back in but for now, it's out and the cut has been feeling correct.


[[Common Sense]] (currently out of the deck) - With 0 copies of Bury, the Common Sense package began to look too small. The flexibility is nice for sure but so far, I haven't been missing it much in testing.



Notable Exclusions:


[[Dream-Quest]] - Even though this deck is looking to keep Tawny around for as long as possible, I don't like that Dream-Quest is mostly dead once you flip Druid. Additionally, the core of this deck is mostly just interchangeable, large minions and removal. Many Druid decks do want Dream-Quest but I don't think that this is one of them.


[[Drums of Doom]] - This deck is already very good at beating minion-heavy aggro decks and I didn't feel like I needed the help of Drums for those matchups. Since this is a deck with lots of large minions that are already going to dominate most combat situations, Drums can end up backfiring really badly for you (particularly against Fire) by allowing your opponents' smaller minions to trade up. Finally, Drums does virtually nothing against Archimago. With all of this in mind, it didn't make sense to include them.



Other Druid lists that I've been tuning:


Sylvan Crusade with a Dash of Fire - With Glastonbury Tor, The Colour out of Space, 3 Funeral Pyre, and Valley of Delight already in the deck, I figured that I could add in a few additional Fire sites and splash for [[Poison Nova]]. Nova is really good with Tawny and Shield Maidens and while I'm not sure that this splash is better than sticking to Earth/Air, it has been working well enough to warrant further testing.


Heavy Meta Druid - This list dips deeper into Fire for things like [[Morgana le Fay]], [[Sir Balin]], [[Sir Kay]], [[Sir Morien]], and [[Pact with the Devil]] while retaining a good amount of the beefy Earth package.


Swamp Song - This is the least tested of my Druid decks and I think also the weakest in the current meta. It uses lots of Water sites to play around Earthquake while tapping into a flexible menagerie of Beasts and Mortals.


The Art of War - A hyper-aggro Fire/Air deck that goes all in on charge minions and splashes for Grapple Shot. Lots of the proximity spells in Fire work nicely with [[Tawny]]!


Druid's Deep - My original Druid deck that is mostly Water with a splash of Air for things like [[Grapple Shot]] and [[Dream-Quest]]. This deck has lots of massive, top-end minions like [[Diluvian Kraken]] and [[Great Old One]].

deckinfo.name: S5 league winner - Grapple Island (40-20)
deckinfo.primer:
Intended for competitive play

*******************************************************************


Overall: This is a control combo deck. Leviathan + graple shot being your 'combo'. The core of the deck is control combo. Dont activate leviathan unless you can at least hit twice. Try to door with leviathan combo by sneaking 4 damage somewhere. Use lightbolt/graple/firebolt/kobolds as finishers.


Note: This is not an easy deck to play. Sometimes you draw the wrong half of your deck against a matchup and lose but site placement can help mitigate that quite a bit.


Matchup Info:

Deathspeaker - slight disadvantage, dont feed them free creatures. Save common sense for early summoning/jihads. play curse on you in the endgame to prevent jhin OTK for a turn or two before they have the mana. Use courtesan to waste their resources once they've started to draw a lot or door them with their own jhin! Non jhin lists are favored.

Sorcerer (Cute/Goblins) - unfavored. Their general gameplan ignores some of your defences. Mariners curse and kobolds are your mvps. It really comes down to if you can draw what you need.

Sorcerer (fury road) - slightly favored. Jihad and a good rift valley will easily tilt it in their favor

Sorcerer (Air/Earth) - slight favored. straightforward matchup

Seer(Yg combo) - playable if you tech for it... If you see seer, dig for common sense/puffer fish early and dont deploy leviathan until pop. If you don't it goes from bad to absolutely terrible.

Other(yg combo) - even / slight advantage. The weakened beatdown/control strategy is something you can easily get ahead of and they will feel safe even with an empty board. Easy to OTK.

Battlemage - Favored, frogs and wheenies stem life lost early. Common sense package destroys artifact based BM.

Avatar earth - Slightly Favored. Displacing your lands puts you on the backfoot early and easily makes up for them having dead removal. The fire variant is harder to deal with as your chumpers die efficiently.

Avatar of air (air only) - Slight disadvantage. The free movement allows their already aggressive deck to be slightly faster. Don't give them free sites to attack or place harmful artifiacts. Muligan aggressively for eggs.

Sorcerer (spirits) - Strong disadvantage/slight disadvantage. Charge and stealth is a problem. If they are running haunts the matchup is even because that deck is a lot worse than big midrange spirits.

Deathspeaker(spirits) - Favored. Clumsy early aggro is easy to chump/deal with and you door them before their top end occurs. Don't feed them free creatures.

Sorcerer/PF(spell control) - Even. Lack of healing means all their spells are good when cast on you unless you draw your eggs. Threats are stick or do something as they come down so its usually always ok to let them die to removal.

Flamespeaker - Even. Can easily lose to great starts (jihad mainly) especially if you don't place your sites correctly

Big water decks - Slight disadvantage. You draw more cards and have decent cards against them. Can't deal with submerge so play around that and it's not bad. Use mariners curse to delay their attacks until they start stockpiling submerge minions. Really its who draws better. You win sideboard hard.

Enchantress (control) - advantage, you have more card advantage and the removal they run generally is reactive while also being threat light. Easy to OTK

Enchantress (aggro/midrange) - slight disadvantage / disadvantage depending on flavor. Some of your removal is hard to use on their threats and often gum up the board.


Mulligans:

-Mulligan lands aggressively for leviathan or threshold if you happen to draw princess in your opener.

-Generally mulligan sites until you hit island leviathan/tadpole pool for placement at site (2).

-Mulligan aggressively for the matchup in the spell card slots but keep obviously (slow) powerful cards if you feel comfortable with the sites you have.

-I generally snap keep princess, curse, land surveyor, and egg


Site placement:

Generally in order of placement

**3 2 3**

4 3 1 3 4


Minor note: Don't play non water sites at 2 or 3 if you are playing something you suspect has rift valley.


1 = dual land / leviathan

2 = bottomless pit / tadpole pool / geistwood ideally / leviathan / any water site

3 = anything, ideally leviathan

4 = non water sites because its easy to protect


General tips:

-You dont win early

-Try to stall your opponent with land placement and chump blockers with the defensive site placement stated above.

- leviathans + graple or a big ruler of thule turn

-try not to activate your leviathans right away unless you can door or the coast is clear (opponent is hellbent or is unlikely to have a good answer)

-Beware of rift valley on a non water site placed forward. Rift valley is the best anything against you.


Specific Tips:

-turtles + manuscript is a draw every turn without it dying.

-Quarrelsome kobolds can safely be placed on the backrow to setup ruler of thule/polar explorer turn

-Kobolds can be used to kill your minions on geistwood if you dont need to block if you opt to run it.

-if you arent feeling extreme pressure and have angels egg + frogs, submerge them so you dont get them disenchanted

-atlantean fate can clutch out your 8 water pips when you draw a lot of non water sites or make it safe to run out leviathans into bury.
